substantial sums of money, thereby putting families under great financial and psychological pressure, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent importance. To my knowledge no political philosophy or party in this House advocates confiscation of private property ownership or rights without appropriate compensation and/or access to due process of law. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That this House categorically reject any legislative initiative such as Bill C-48, or policy direction by government which advocates or incorporates into the laws of Parliament retroactive expropriation by government, or Crown corporations of government, of property deemed to be private property without due compensation and/or access to due process of law.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, for the second day in a row, after his well-touted meetings in Washington concerning the ailing auto industry, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who assured us that he would be in his seat yesterday and today, is still not here. I find that highly irresponsible on his part.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESULTS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Therefore, in the minister's absence, since the acting minister did not know what was going on yesterday, I would like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. Could the Prime Minister tell this House his views on the $4.5 billion auto pact deficit which has been experienced by the Canadian auto industry and the 94 per cent increase in imported Japanese automobiles coming in to this country? What decisions were reached in Washington in the numerous meetings that the minister has had, on which, in his irresponsibility, he has

April 14, 1981

not come to the House, nor has he given us even one of his famous press releases as to the outcome of these meetings? What decisions were made as a result of the meetings in Washington last week?

As I pointed out to him yesterday, the hon. member is aware that the government has spared no effort to solve the problems of the Chrysler Corporation. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see that the great Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has made a courageous entry into the House of Commons-
Hear, hear!

-to tell us about his conquests in Washington last week, since none of the other cabinet ministers knew what was going on.
My supplementary question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In view of the 94 per cent increase in Japanese auto imports into Canada over last year and the continuing failure of the minister to negotiate a consensus among Japanese manufacturers which would guarantee voluntary restrictions of exports of automobiles to Canada, can the minister tell us, notwithstanding his reluctance to impose temporary import quotas, what considerations, if any, have been given to using Japanese dependency on our natural resources as a lever to urge Japan's auto manufacturers to include at least some Canadian, or a higher Canadian, content in parts made in their production of automobiles, and for that matter a higher degree of investment in the Canadian auto parts and manufacturing sector? Has this position been taken with the Japanese? If not, why not? What is the minister waiting for?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my discussions with the Japanese, which began last year, I pointed out to them that our exports to that country were composed of a relatively small, in fact a too small, proportion of manufactured goods. I expressed the view that it would be in the interests of the healthy continuation of our trade with Japan that a better and larger portion of it would be in the form of manufactured goods.
I would be very interested to have my hon. friend confirm that it is the policy of his party, including the Conservative members from western Canada, to put the exports of resources from that part of our country to Japan on the block in the way that he suggested.

speechtext: Not only did the minister not answer that question, he has still not told us what decisions were made in Washington in his talks last week. It is very obvious that the minister is not taking this matter seriously, but I can assure him that we are, and that hundreds of thousands of Canadians who depend on a healthy auto industry in Canada are, as well.
Quit skating!

My last supplementary question is this: last week the minister said, and I quote very quickly, "We're not talking about joint decisions", with the United States. "We're talking about making our own decisions." That is what we have been asking as well. The minister has a number of specific recommendations and a number of specific options. Can he tell us now why he has not taken action on these specific recommendations and options, and when can the industry and when can Canadians expect some of these specific decisions to be made?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We have taken a number of specific decisions aimed at strengthening the position of the auto industry, its workers, and the firms in it in our country. My hon. friend was giving these details as I came into the House-the agreement with respect to Chrysler which protects thousands of jobs in this country, both in Chrysler itself and in hundreds of supplying firms; our agreement with Ford with respect to the future of the Oakville plant; the discussions we completed which led to the reopening of the Ford foundry in Windsor; the assistance with respect to the aluminum engine, at the Essex (Engine) plant.
With respect to the situation in Japan, we have already been talking to the Japanese and have said to them that we expect they will give us the same type of administrative guidance with respect to exports to Canada that they are giving with respect to exports to the United States.
We have a team in Japan right now to make sure that the Japanese understand that if they take action with respect to exports of cars to the United States, there must be equivalent action with respect to exports to Canada. If that is not done, and there is a diversionary situation with respect to exports of Japanese cars to our country, we will have to take action
April 14, 1981

within our own legal framework, in the light of our own market situation, in order to assure the position of the Canadian industry and the Canadian workers. So we have been taking concrete action, and we are prepared to take further concrete action in the interests of the industry, its workers, and the entire Canadian economy.

Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF SPRING BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister which concerns the economic crisis that Canada is currently going through. We now have more than one million people unemployed and the numbers are growing; the cost of living has increased some 12 per cent year over year and the situation is worsening. The government's budget forecasts have turned out to be completely wrong.
My question to the Prime Minister, who is responsible for the government as a whole, is as follows: now that the constitutional debate is almost completed, will he show that he is concerned about unemployment and about the cost of living by announcing the government's intention to bring in a new budget when the House resumes on May 12?

subsubtopic: PLANS TO ASSIST PARTS SUPPLY SECTOR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As the minister well knows, the falling off in demand for cars and trucks in Canada has resulted in lay-offs in the industry, with perhaps a greater degree of lay-off in the auto parts manufacturing industry. In view of the recent announcement that Japanese car imports have increased by 94 per cent over last year and with the minister's own comment that he will not act against those imports, what assurance will he give that we in Canada will continue to have a parts supply industry? What alternative plan of action will he initiate for those persons who are subject to the present lay-offs and those that they can expect in years to come?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PLANS TO ASSIST PARTS SUPPLY SECTOR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have not ruled out any options. We are continuing to keep all options under active review. We are monitoring the situation very closely.
With respect to the auto parts sector, the efforts we are making are linked with assisting them to increase their sales in foreign markets, including countries like Japan, through trading missions, through assistance to trade fairs and activities of that sort. We are working with the auto parts sector through the Enterprise Development Program to help them get the capital they require in order to re-tool and re-equip.
Our efforts to facilitate the restructuring of the major vehicle manufacturers in this country are aimed also at not only facilitating their ongoing activity but at increasing the opportunities for the independent parts sector to have growing outlets for their manufacturers with the major manufacturers, so as to maintain and strengthen employment opportunities in the parts sector. The concerns and opportunities of that sector are very much part of our strategy and our efforts.

subsubtopic: PLANS TO ASSIST PARTS SUPPLY SECTOR
speechtext: Since the minister has clearly made a statement with respect to imports, will he not now answer clearly and distinctly whether he will initiate a requirement for Canadian content in imported cars sold in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PLANS TO ASSIST PARTS SUPPLY SECTOR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is one of the aspects we have under review. It was one of the ideas presented to us at the major meeting with the industry we had last week. We do have Canadian value added requirements on the part of the motor vehicle manufacturers now as part of the arrangements under the auto pact. We are interested not only in maintaining but increasing the use of Canadian components in automobiles assembled here and sold in world markets. This is a very important part of our strategy and objective for the industry.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the debate closed last Thursday evening on Bill C-42, to establish the Canada Post Corporation, I was speaking about two areas of concern to the New Democratic Party in respect to this new Crown corporation. One concern was with regard to small contractors and the fact that this new Crown corporation will deny them the right to become members of a union to negotiate their agreements. That is a matter we discussed quite firmly in committee, and I should like to quote from the remarks of the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), as reported in the Proceedings and Minutes of the committee for December 18, 1980, as follows:
The present land mail service contracts that we have are valued at about $90 million. If we were to carry this to the extreme-and I do not want to exaggerate the figure-the possibility of increased expenditures could be doubled or even tripled.
I wonder what the Labour Relations Board would think of a private business which was denying its workers the right to become unionized because it was simply too expensive? I am sure the Labour Relations Board would take a very dim view of that.

The other area of concern we have in respect of this bill relates to telecommunications operations. In the original bill the minister brought before the committee there were provisions for the new Crown corporation to become very actively involved in telecommunications as they relate to postal matters. Members of multinationals came in large numbers-I think they gathered as many as 20 in one group-before the committee and lobbied against the corporation's becoming actively involved in this area. With the help of the Conservative party and some members of the Liberal Party, groups including IT&T, Xerox, Kodak and Bell Canada, as well as our favourites, the insurance companies and the banks, convinced the Postmaster General that these provisions should be excluded and that they should so have the right. On behalf of our party, I am very disappointed that the minister folded under the pressure and that the new bill leaves this field wide open to multinationals from other areas.
I think this is a sad day for Canada and Canadians because this is going to be the way of the future in the post office. In five or ten years we will look back at this bill and say that we as Canadians lost something we should have provided for in the bill, and that we should then have started to gear ourselves up for the future.
For a moment I would like to speak to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), respecting what is known as a sunset clause. He said there was not time in committee to put it forward. It is correct that a sunset clause which could possibly be looked at five years down the road was never mentioned in committee. The Conservative Party should have spent a little more time with those kinds of programs instead of worrying about courier services, insurance companies and large multinationals. Very little was said about daily postal services in committee, yet they rise in the House and speak about it time after time. We all know that postal services are bad in every riding and that something must be done about the situation. That is what we are trying to do in this bill; we are trying to establish a corporation which will operate under some good management.
I should like to talk about the management of this new Crown corporation. The minister said that the management would be comprised of representatives from labour, management and Canada at large. It will be important for the government to select the very best people it can. I think the government should consult the Canadian Labour Congress and try to obtain some of the very best labour-oriented people to help bring this corporation together in a fair way. I hope the government is able to find a top management person who understands the operations and working atmosphere of the corporation. It will be very, very important for the directors of this board to bring about, in a very aggressive and determined way, a new service and a new program for the Crown corporation.
In closing, we urge the speedy passage of this bill, despite the reservations which I have just outlined. We are convinced
Canada Post Corporation Act
that it is in the best interests of Canada to establish this Crown corporation as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make some brief comments regarding this bill, particularly an amendment which was made at committee level. It is my understanding that at committee level it was possible to make provision for a reasonable opportunity for appeal by local citizens when there is closure of a postal service. This provision would be with respect to shutdowns, cutbacks or closures. It is a good provision. As the bill is written, a reasonable opportunity for appeal includes the fact that any regulation closing down a postal station, for example, would have to go to cabinet. This is a legislative improvement of the present situation.
Presently when the government moves to close local postal services, the decision does not have to go to cabinet, at least not by way of legislation. While I feel that provision is good in principle, I appeal to the government that the practice and the implementation of that particular clause should be equally as good.
In speaking to that area, I should like to use an ongoing example in my riding. The government announced the closing down of a postal service in the city of Winnipeg, Postal Station D providing full postal service and substituting for it a sub post office in a drugstore. Clearly it will not be possible for people to receive the same service from a very small counter within a portion of a drugstore as they would receive from a full postal station in the neighbourhood.
The principle in this legislation should be put in practice now, before the bill is passed. The residents of Winnipeg who are served by Postal Station D should be given a reasonable opportunity to appeal the decision to close down this postal station. By "a reasonable opportunity", I mean they should have available to them the time in which to make a proper appeal and the information needed.
We have written to the government about this matter. We have moved motions in the House requesting the studies or information upon which this decision was based, but it was to no avail. We have not received any justification from the government for Postal Station D being shut down.
We contend that a reasonable opportunity to appeal such a closure should include providing the studies on which the government has made its decision, so that the community can question the studies and offer alternative information. Then cabinet could look at this service to the community and say, "Let us make a balanced decision in this case; let us have all the facts before us."
One reason offered by way of speculation on this station's being closed is that there is no other building in this very large urban neighbourhood in which to house a postal station. The present lease on the building has run out, and the government claims that it cannot find another building in the area to rent in order to continue that postal service. Clearly this is unsatisfactory. It is a complete misrepresentation of the nature of the neighbourhood. There are adequate buildings in the area. I

wish the government would not use such a flimsy excuse for a cutback in services.
I do not have before me the basis upon which the government made the decision to cut back this service. This is why I ask the government to hold off the closing of Postal Station D which is scheduled for April 24 and to provide the information so that the community can conduct a proper appeal.
I could guess at possible reasons why the government might close down a postal station. For example, the government might feel that it would save money by way of staff or the rental of space. But I must say that there are no savings in terms of staff in this particular case. The staff will be transferred out of the local postal station to the central postal station, so the government will still have to pay for staff. The space required for the local postal station and its many activities will be transferred to other locations, so the government will still have to pay for space.
Also I suggest that adequate revenues are generated by the postal service in the neighbourhood to support local services. If I had the financial analysis upon which the government decided to cut back the service, I could make a clear criticism of it, but I would like to make a couple of suggestions about possible revenues. Meter settings have been transferred out of this area. This is a very lucrative source of revenue and could support a local postal station. Lock boxes in the neighbourhood would be a source of revenue to keep the station open. In fact, in the downtown and centralized location in the city there are lock boxes. Their numbers are being increased and there is a three-month waiting period. Yet there is not even the space in the downtown central postal station to accommodate additional lock boxes to meet the local demand. So why not decentralize throughout the neighbourhoods in the city and reap the revenues which there will be by way of providing lock box services rather than simply depriving the postal station of these revenues and depriving the neighbourhoods of any local community service?
As I have said, lock boxes would be a possible source of revenue. I have been informed that a private company has opened up a lock box service in the neighbourhood of Postal Station D. I have a letter before me from the Canadian Union of Postal Workers in Winnipeg which reads in part:
-a private company has opened up a lock box service in the area of Postal Station D-
Is this some sort of continued privatization plan on behalf of the government, turning over public services to the private sector so that the private sector can reap the profit at the expense of the local community? There is clearly a demand here for lock box services. There is a demand for a service which could produce a revenue and for a continuation of neighbourhood services which people find convenient to use.
If I had the study before me upon which the government decided to discontinue this service, I could examine the facts with regard to revenues and expenditures. At this point I am
simply forced to speculate on the reasons which were used to justify the closure of this postal station. This action is not in the spirit of the legislation which is before us. The spirit of the legislation before us is much better than that of the present administration of the government. The government should live up to the spirit of the legislation, immediately halt the closure of Postal Station D in Winnipeg and give the residents a clear and reasonable opportunity to appeal the decision to close.
I would like to say that the letters which I have received from the minister's office in response to my letters have not even been signed by the minister, so the minister has not really looked at this situation, and neither has cabinet. The new legislation would require that before a postal station such as this was closed down, cabinet would have to make a decision. We are seeing a level of attention from this government which falls far short of what the legislation intends. I would have liked this legislation to pass much earlier than now so that people in my riding would be protected by it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-42, which is an act to establish the Canada Post Corporation, to repeal the Post Office Act and other related acts and to make related amendments to other acts.
I could not help but be upset by the remarks of the previous speaker. I think all of us in this House recognize the valuable work done by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) who has worked so hard to create a postal Crown corporation. He had a commitment from the former prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), to bring in a bill to convert the Post Office into a Crown corporation by the spring of 1980. For the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) to suggest that we are holding up this legislation is ridiculous, to say the least.
This bill was introduced last October for second reading. It was discussed in the House on October 24 and October 28. It was then delayed by this government until November 20. It is not the opposition which decides what legislation can be presented to the House and when it can be presented. That is the government's responsibility; no one else in this House has delayed this legislation. It is the obligation of the opposition to debate, probe and amend any proposed legislation which comes before the House. For a member of the New Democratic Party to stand up and say that we are delaying legislation is anything but the truth.
Bill C-42 went to committee on November 25. We debated the proposed bill in committee on that date and on the following dates: November 27, December 1, 4, 9, 10, 11, 15, 16, 17 and 18. It is a very complicated bill. Everyone recognizes the benefits which will accrue to the public by converting the Post Office into a Crown corporation. Surely anyone who attended the committee meetings understood the complexity of the bill.
The bill was brought back to the House on April 8. We have an hon. member in the NDP saying that we delayed it. There is only one hon. member in this House who can bring any legislation before this House, and that is the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). The only person who tells him when to bring it before this House is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). If there is anyone delaying legislation, it is the Liberal party, no one else.
For many weeks we have been asking for legislation to be brought forward, to get on with matters and suspend the constitutional debate. We knew there were important matters
Canada Post Corporation Act
besides the Post Office, the economy and inflation, but the government refused to bring measures forward. Third reading began on April 9, and continues today, April 14. We also are anxious to have this bill go through, but we are not going to give this government a blank cheque.
There were provisions in the bill which were harmful to the public, and we have attempted to change some of them. Unfortunately, the government, with its majority and with the support of the NDP, was able to override our amendments.
The Post Office affects all of us. There is not one person here who is not affected by the post office every day in his life. Senior citizens are constantly sending us letters saying: "I do not get my letters on time. When am I going to get my mail? What are you going to do about the fact that I do not get postal delivery to my door?"
People are moving from Ontario to Calgary, buying a home, moving in, and finding out that they will not get any mail delivery for anywhere from two to five years. They are not being told that by the Post Office or by the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet). Then when they take the time to go down to the local post office to try to find out why, they are finally told, "We're sorry, there is a freeze on; we cannot help you". However, the Post Office does not provide any information telling people, they cannot have postal service. They keep quiet about that.
Numerous studies have been brought forward on the Post Office. I would like to refer to just a few of them. The first recommendations in this regard were made in 1962 by the Glassco commission and by the Montpetit commission. In December, 1978, Bill C-27 was introduced. It died on the Order Paper. In 1974 the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) was preparing to bring forth a bill to make the Post Office into a Crown corporation.
When one looks back at the history of the Post Office, one is astounded by some of the things which have happened. Between 1918 and 1965 there were three strikes in the Post Office. The people of Canada were without mail for seven weeks. Between 1968 and 1978 there were 11 Post Office strikes in Canada. However, that is not the worst part. A strike is one thing, but would one believe that as a result of the 11 strikes the people of Canada were without mail service for 51 weeks? In the last 13 years we have been without mail service for one full year. Then the government had the gall, supported by the NDP, to suggest we are holding this bill up. They should hang their heads in shame. We want to examine this bill to make sure that it is a viable bill and that the people can live with it. It is ridiculous to suggest that we are holding up passage of this bill.
There is some sad history relating to this bill. In 1967-68 the average cost of a piece of mail, regardless of size, was eight cents. The cost has now risen to 27 cents for the average piece of mail. In 1968-69 the Post Office lost $67 million. Last year it lost $279 million. It now looks as though it will lose $450 million.

April 14, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
It is interesting to look at some of the figures. In 1968 there were 36,000 workers in the post office; there are now over
60,000,	an increase of 64 per cent. However, in 1968 each worker handled 132,000 items a year; now, according to the latest figures, they handle 106,000. There must be something the matter with the way in which the Post Office is operating. We know there are problems between the unions and the workers.
In speaking to Post Office officials from time to time, I have referred to some of the ridiculous expenditures by the Post Office. In the post office in Calgary and, I assume, in many of the other supposedly modern ones, there is an optical character reader. I am not sure what it costs now, but to upgrade it will cost something over a million dollars. I have written to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) asking him when this would happen. The Post Office management are crying out for these OCRs. The optical character reader has an efficiency ratio of 78 per cent and it replaces approximately 20 people. It operates at 50 per cent of capacity. Twenty people replace the optical character reader instead of 40. In other words, they need 20 more people in the Post Office than really necessary. What do those 20 people represent? It is almost ridiculous to go through the mathematics. Twenty people at $20,000 a year is $400,000. In a little over two years they could pay for the OCR. However, the Post Office supposedly imposed a freeze. The real problem is that it does not know how to make decisions. It cannot get any leadership from the Postmaster General; he would rather sit back and wait until somebody else moves in and tries to solve the problem.
We are aware that there are problems in the Post Office between the unions and the workers. The NDP does not like anyone to say that. It is quite evident that there are problems. There are also problems between the unions and management. One union leader has said, "I don't care if the Post Office ever works; I am not here for the Post Office". All one has to do is to ask, and he will say why he does not care.
There are problems with management and staff because the union sits between them and they do not know what to do. There is trouble between the two unions and between the inside and outside workers. Although there are a number of problems, it is hoped that by making the Post Office a Crown corporation some of them will be solved.
I should now like to refer to my own riding. The conditions there are a disgrace. There are approximately 4,000 homes without any type of mail delivery. I have tried to explain to the Postmaster General, the deputy postmaster general and the regional postmasters that this involves unbelievable cost. Some of these people have to drive up to five miles a day to collect their mail. As I explained to them, the cost for gas alone is over $200,000 per year. They keep saying that they cannot afford to do anything about it, but it is costing some people $200,000 per year. If the figures that I get from the Post Office are correct, the average postman can handle up to 500 homes. Therefore, it would require eight postal officers, eight
postal workers, to handle the 4,000 homes in my riding that are without service. At a cost of $30,000 each worker, the total would come to less than a quarter of a million dollars.
This government does not know how to save money, Mr. Speaker; it only knows how to spend it. We should question everything that it brings forward to this House. We might agree with its legislation, but we are bound to examine it because we do not know what the government will try to slide through.
From time to time in this House I have risen to ask the minister some questions. On June 5, 1980, I put a question to him; on May 16, 1980, I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 and on June 26, 1980, I spoke on the adjournment debate. The questions that I brought up at those times have never been answered by the Postmaster General. He says, "Wait until it becomes a Crown corporation and we will solve all those problems".
About a month and a half ago, in reply to a question put by one of my colleagues, the minister said that for each letter that might be delivered late, 90 or 92 arrived on time. Being fairly well acquainted with the Post Office, I decided to check that out. I called the Ottawa postal station and was told that it takes two or three days for a letter to go from Ottawa to Calgary. We did an analysis and found that of 102 letters sent to Calgary from my office in February, six were delivered within four days; 25 within five days; 43 within six days; 12 within seven days; eight within eight days; six within 11 days; one within 12 days; one within 13 days and none on time. I would challenge the Postmaster General to prove that 90 or 92 letters out of 93 reach their destination on time. The minister made that statement off the top of his head.
In my constituency office the greatest problem I have by far is the non-delivery of mail. Pay is not received on time by union staff. They even have trouble with their unions and cannot get satisfaction there. There are problems between the union and the staff over pay. Many inside postal workers do not receive their pay sometimes for up to six weeks. What does the Postmaster General do about that? It is no wonder that we want to examine this bill. If we did not examine it, our constituents would be asking us why we can trust whatever the government brings forward. Obviously this government brings forward things which the public cannot abide.
I am as anxious to have the Post Office made into a Crown corporation as anyone else, but I think we must remember one very important point. This Crown corporation must be responsible to Parliament. The Post Office is in a mess but it did not get that way by itself; it got there because of inept ministers, past and present. I hope that the Postmaster General will keep in mind that one of the main ways to prevent the same thing from happening again is to have the Auditor General audit the books of the Post Office. If we do not ensure that happens, we will be remiss in our duties.
I am as anxious to see the work of the hon. member for Vancouver South completed as anyone. We hope to get the bill through, but I must tell the Postmaster General that of all

Crown corporations present and future, we will be keeping a closer eye on the new post corporation than on any other.

I want to draw hon. members' attention to an organization which is active in my riding. It is called N-TEC, which stands for Niagara Training and Employment Agency Inc. N-TEC is located in Port Robinson, Ontario. The agency is a non-profit, vocational, rehabilitation workshop providing programs and services for the emotionally, mentally and physically disabled adults of the Niagara region. Currently, approximately 75 people are employed in their program. One of the vocational training programs they operate involves the delivery of bills for a number of public and private utility corporations in the Niagara region. I have visited this institution. I must say I am impressed with the facilities they have and with the staff who work with these people. This is a place where retarded and disabled people can find meaningful employment. They gain self-respect, create a self-image and learn resourcefulness. As a result they feel needed and wanted. N-TEC is heavily dependent on the revenues generated by the mail delivery program.
It seems that this program will be lost. N-TEC will be extremely hard pressed to meet all its obligations and will certainly suffer financial hardship as a result. In the light of the current economic climate, they doubt whether they could secure other contracts to recover the possible loss of mail delivery contracts which they have had. Indeed, it will be a severe blow to N-TEC.
Aside from the monetary issues, of course, the more critical issue is that of people, to which I alluded just a minute ago. People with disabilities have faced disadvantages throughout their lives. N-TEC's purpose is to try to even the score and provide opportunity where it did not exist. N-TEC gives people a chance to produce and therefore contribute to their own well-being as well as to society. The people at N-TEC do contribute. They take a great deal of pride in themselves and for the reliable and dependable service for which that organization is known. It is true there are jobs which disabled people cannot perform, but then there are many more jobs they can. Invoice delivery happens to be one of them, with the added bonus that these people can learn to work in their own community with their heads held high by the recognition they have earned.
Restoring self-dignity is the first step forward. That can only take place if meaningful work exists for these people. In this International Year of the Handicapped, should we not be thinking of ways to assist, not hinder, our disabled people? In the total scheme of things N-TEC's invoice delivery contracts are only a drop in what we might call the proverbial bucket. Whom are we hurting if we continue what has begun? They are not asking for a handout, a loan, a grant or even a parliamentary decree; in fact, they ask for nothing. The disabled ask for nothing but the right to be ordinary people.
What we need in this House, and what needs to be displayed by this government, is justice, justice tempered with mercy. I want to put on the record excerpts from two letters which I

Surety the loss of revenue to the post office that this small band of willing, handicapped workers would cause would be a "drop in the bucket" when compared to the total revenue of the post office department.
I could plead, Mr. Prime Minister, further that this is the International Year of the Handicapped. Mr. Speaker, I too will be brief. The space shuttle astronauts had to make their decisions in split seconds during their magnificent re-entry and landing today. Therefore, ten minutes should be sufficient to get my point across. I have my stop watch set.
I welcome the opportunity to speak briefly before this House on a very important piece of legislation, Bill C-42, which seeks to create the Canada Post Corporation. I want to assure this House at the outset that I support and welcome a Crown corporation for the Post Office.
As member of Parliament for Hamilton-Wentworth, I have had the opportunity many times to present the Postmaster General with numerous cases of very poor postal service to many of my constituents. In some cases I have been satisfied that the Postmaster General's answers were fair and well researched. I hope the Postmaster General is listening at the moment because I am going to pay a rare compliment to him. speechtext:
Now for the bad news. I have to admit that in the majority of cases when I have contacted the Postmaster General, frankly I have not been satisfied with the answers he has given me, either in this House
April 14, 1981

of Commons or through correspondence. Nor have I been satisfied with the Postmaster General's role in this House.
The hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and I have known each other for a long time. We have a good working relationship when he wears his other hat as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. However, that is the problem: he wears too darned many hats.
I believe the Postmaster General is being spread far too thin for his various duties to be effective. In addition to his onerous role as head of the Post Office, perhaps one of the most difficult and thankless jobs, he is also splitting his time as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In addition to these weighty responsibilities, the minister has a heavy schedule as Quebec lieutenant of his party. The clearest indication that the minister is spread too thin is easily documented by the often uninformed answers he provides the House of Commons, even after I have briefed him from time to time on questions I would like to ask him as consumer affairs minister. However, I feel he has a handle on that department through his officials.
I hope once the new Canada Post Corporation is born that a different minister will be assigned to speak for that Crown corporation in the House. It will give the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs more time to spend, which I think he knows he needs to spend, on the very important area of consumer and corporate affairs.
May I deal briefly with another problem within the Post Office other than that of the minister, namely, the deplorable state of management-labour relations. We constantly hear of ongoing chaos and confusion through the media, through our work in the House and through our constituents. I cannot think of another institution or private company in Canada which enjoys or suffers worse relations.
This would seem to strike at the heart of our problem in our current postal system. There is precious little, if any, trust from either labour's or management's point of view. As long as this situation is allowed to continue, the Post Office, either as a government department or a Crown corporation, will not function effectively.
However, the problem is not primarily labour-oriented. A number of my constituents are Post Office employees. They are dedicated, do their jobs well and are proud of the valuable work they do in the time-honoured tradition of Canada's royal mail. They are frustrated, however, by the attitude of management. They are frustrated by the introduction of machinery, which has been done haphazardly without regard for those working on it. They are frustrated with a system of management where it takes two to three months to receive overtime pay. They are frustrated by a system of management which has refused to take employees' grievances seriously.
Just as management will take an intransigent attitude, so will employees. I firmly believe that if we transfer the same management personnel currently in the Post Office to the Crown corporation, just as if we automatically transfer the trouble-makers in certain sections of the Post Office to a
Canada Post Corporation Act
Crown corporation, we will simply be transferring the problem, not eliminating it. We must be able to get the Post Office as a Crown corporation organized so that we can finally move the mail quickly, effectively and efficiently. We cannot sit back and hope that this is all going to happen; we are going to have to work at it.
People ask what good it is going to do by turning the Post Office into a Crown corporation. Good question. There are good Crown corporations and there are bad ones. We on this side of the House are going to ensure that the Canada Post Corporation will be a good one. We will be watching it very closely.
Aside from the management-labour concerns, the Canadian people in general, and certainly the citizens in my riding of Hamilton-Wentworth, are concerned with the length of time it takes to get the mail delivered. We have heard a litany of disasters throughout this debate from members on all sides of this House regarding these problems.
The Postmaster General states that 95 per cent of the mail is being delivered on time. To put it mildly, my people think this estimate perhaps a wee bit high. I receive on average two letters per week complaining about the postal system and many more phone calls. I guess a lot of people simply do not trust the mail. Let me describe just three of the most recent letter complaints I have received. A letter from the Canadian Pension Commission here in Ottawa was mailed on February 2, 1981, to a constituent of mine in Hamilton. It was delivered on February 19, 1981. I find it very hard to understand why it took a first-class letter complete with postal code 17 days to get from Ottawa to Hamilton.
Another case in point is from Mrs. Howell of Jerseyville, Ontario. A reply to a request of Mrs. Howell's was mailed in Toronto on December 17, 1980 and delivered on January 14, 1981. Jerseyville is roughly 45 miles from Toronto. It would have been quicker to hand deliver it. I could have delivered it.
Mrs. Goodram of Ancaster, Ontario, had a very important letter to send to her son in Calgary. She decided to register it, thinking it would get to its destination in good order and plenty of time. She mailed it on December 22, 1980. The registered letter finally reached Calgary on January 21, 1981. You can talk about the Christmas mail rush and all the delays that entails; however, for a registered letter to take that length of time to travel half way across Canada is unforgivable.
I will not go into the countless letters complaining that it took 25 days for mail to arrive from Britain or into the delays in getting mail to Dundas, Ontario, from Ancaster, Ontario- both in my riding-a distance of less than five miles. I do not even want to go into the case of the letter which went from Ancaster to Dundas via London, England. The current record, apparently, from Ancaster to Dundas is nine days. Nine days! That is the record for the Post Office. Do hon. members see why we want a Crown corporation? The service can only improve.

We all know the frustration of dealing with parcel post. If we receive a parcel within a few weeks, the odds are even that it will be damaged. I recently received eight packages from various provincial capitals across Canada. They were provincial flags which we were to instal at 447 Squadron at Mount Hope. Half the package had been repaired by Canada Post. The parcel-sorting machines simply chewed those packages up and spit them out. Mercifully, the flags arrived intact.
Two constituents of mine, Mike and Wendy Gould, went out to visit western Canada. While in Nelson, British Columbia, they purchased some unique stoneware pottery. Unable to bring it home through the airline, they decided-with much trepidation, I might add-to put their faith in Canada Post. Well, you guessed it; even though they packed it very carefully-they absolutely plastered it with "Fragile" stickers-and registered it, the thing was delivered smashed to pieces. The district post office said, "Sorry, we can't be responsible for damage incurred," even though it was properly packaged, properly marked and properly insured. Hon. members may ask, as I did, why on earth they would entrust their valued pottery to the Post Office. They wanted to use the Post Office, not some private courier, because day after day we are told to have faith in and use our postal service.
What happens when you have a small business and must rely on the parcel post system for movement of goods? Let us consider the case of Mr. Paul Orosz of Hamilton, Ontario, who has a small car radio business. He occasionally must return units to the manufacturer. Last summer, after successfully using the mails before, he mailed on three separate occasions from two different postal stations three properly wrapped, marked and insured parcels for return to the manufacturer. All three packages where smashed when they reached their destination. Mr. Orosz was presented with a bill of $377 for repairing those radios. We found out later that the parcels were insured for theft only, not damage. Mr. Orosz used the mail because, like many other small businesses, he could not afford courier or freight rates. But he will use these in the future. What is the cost to Canada Post and the new Crown corporation if many more people like the Goulds or Mr. Orosz decide not to use the postal system again?
We are having a difficult time getting proper mail delivery in some sections of my riding. These are rural areas which have been served by the same post office for many years now. An elderly couple ran one post office but they have declined to continue. The officials in that area have not been able to find anyone to carry out the job, so they are attempting to get some other type of service, such as box service or door to door delivery. This is also happening in one special community in my riding, West Flamborough. It is an area with a great number of elderly Canadians. Service must be accessible in the winter months or in just plain poor weather. A decision has not yet been reached. The minister has assured me, however, that action will be taken-or that at least this can be more fairly, efficiently and properly dealt with-when Bill C-42 is given final assent.
Although I feel there may be an axe being held over my head, the people in my riding deserve a postal system which is efficient, reasonable and improved over the present one, and so we are waiting for the birth of the Canada Post Corporation.
In connection with this legislation, I am returning it to the sender; but I will be supporting this bill to make the Post Office a Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a considerable pleasure for me to rise to indicate the support of my party for the legislation which is before the House. As all hon. members know, as postmaster general I was committed, on behalf of my party, to introduce this legislation as early as the late spring of 1980.1 want it shown on the record that that was accepted by the prime minister at that time, and I have to say to those who have spoken of delay that the delay is not due to any acts of the government of the leader of my party.
I also have to say, because it is appropriate to do so, that while I was occupying the post of postmaster general I received very considerable co-operation from all of the unions which represent the workers in the Post Office, and I also received co-operation from the managerial part of the Post Office. At my request I received very considerable co-operation from the Canadian Labour Congress, which agreed to oversee a committee which would work toward the implementation of a bill which, as far as possible, would meet the needs of management and the postal workers. I know my friend, the present Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), received continuing co-operation from that Canadian Labour Congress committee.
The whole thrust of the bill I was working on and the thrust of this bill is to give a new chance to the Post Office and the Post Office family. I believe the bill recognizes in a very significant way the necessity to continue this great public service for all Canadians, not just a limited number of them. While the bill presented to the House is no doubt not without some defects, it goes a long way toward meeting the needs not only of the Post Office but also of the Canadian public, which is entitled to service from the Post Office.
I regret that I have to bring to the attention of hon. members a letter which was written by a friend of mine in the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), but I am going to mention it. I hope my friend, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), who has worked as the NDP critic on matters relating to the Post Office, will not take anything I say as being aimed at him because I assure the hon. member that these remarks are made only with respect to this letter; I impute nothing to my hon. friend, who has worked extremely closely with me and has contributed very greatly to the improvement of this bill.
Again I say I regret having to bring this to the attention of hon. members, but on March 24, 1981, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway wrote a letter to a gentleman in Vancouver in which he said this:
Unfortunately, we have been unable to get all-party agreement for this very important piece of legislation.
April 14, 1981

He was referring to Bill C-42.
The Conservative Party has decided to stall the changes, mainly because the new Crown corporation is likely to hurt some of their corporate friends in the courier business. Although the bill was ready to be implemented as early as last fall-
The fall of 1980.
-the Tories have succeeded in keeping it off the floor of the House of Commons for almost six months.
I understand the cut and thrust of politics, but I do not understand a written statement which does not contain a grain of truth. I regret this very much because the hon. member is well and very favourably known to me. I suspect he did not even write the letter, but it is certainly clear that he signed it. I hope hon. members will bear with me for just a minute while I put the record straight.
First of all, the bill was introduced in July, 1980. Marin, commissioner of inquiry relating to the security and investigation of services branch within the Post Office Department.

Other groups that submitted briefs which were looked at by the committee include Action Bell Canada, the Canadian Business Equipment Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Direct Mail Marketing Association, the Canadian Industrial Communications Assembly, the Magazine Association of Canada, the Ontario Trucking Association, General Motors of Canada Limited, V.S. Services Limited, the Canadian Cable Television Association, Peter R. Kemball & Associates and the United Parcel Service Canada Limited.
I do not think I need gild the lily here, except to point out that all these groups which came before us have a very real interest in the Post Office and in the legislation which is before us. It does some credit to the members of the committee-and I give credit where credit is due to members of the committee on all sides, to the Postmaster General and my friend, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke, and also colleagues of mine-that in a space of seven days all those witnesses were heard. Because they worked long hours, the bill came out of the committee in a form to be presented to the House of Commons very late on the night of December 18. The bill was released from committee that night because there was a very real sense on my part and on the part of others that, in view of the labour negotiations which were taking place at the time, all haste should be used within the bounds of common sense to get the bill through. As a consequence the bill was then released from committee and brought back to the House for report stage and third reading. It was not introduced to the House at the report stage until April 7. The blame for that, if one wants to lay blame, can only lie with the government. It certainly was not my party that was trying to hold up the bill.
I am sorry to dwell on this, Mr. Speaker, but I feel the accusation made in the letter of the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway is so false the public is entitled to have an answer to it.
When the bill came before the House there were 11 motions at report stage, and they were dealt with expeditiously. It is interesting to note that three of the motions put forward by my party were accepted by the Postmaster General, and one was ruled out of order. Three of the government motions were accepted while four of the motions put forward by my party were rejected. One of those motions was supported by my colleagues in the NDP. That was the very important amendment, which we wish had been accepted by the government, relating to the necessity to appoint the Auditor General as auditor for the Crown corporation. Hon. members will remember that the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke spoke very strongly in support of that proposal and NDP members voted with us.
In respect of the rest of the debate, it has gone on for several days and I am happy to advise the House that it is going to end this afternoon.
I just want to say a couple of things. First of all, as my friend the hon. Postmaster General knows, just creating the Crown corporation is not in itself the whole answer to the problems of the Post Office. It is a start and it has to be given a chance. I hope the government, after this bill is passed with

April 14, 1981
Adjournment Motion
our support, will be extremely careful in the appointment of the board of directors. The Postmaster General knows that the number on the board of directors was expanded at our suggestion, with his consent and compliance.
It is also important that there be some continuation of management personnel. Having had some experience in that respect, I can assure all hon. members it will be extremely important to maintain continuity of management during the transition stage, at least until the Post Office is actually operating in full swing as a Crown corporation.
The other thing I want to say, and I will close on this, Mr. Speaker, is that there are many people who, because they are frustrated and as a consequence are criticial of the Post Office, perhaps unintentionally though sometimes intentionally, tend to leave the impression that we should just break it up and disband it because surely somebody else could perform the service. I want to address that matter by referring to only a few points.
The Post Office is a great Canadian public institution. There is no way the service which Canadians all over this great land require can be handled by just taking parts of the post office operation and turning them over to private corporations. I am convinced that if that were done the easy traffic would be handled at great profit but the difficult and costly traffic would not be handled at all. If the Post Office is to succeed, it must be able to compete for the profitable traffic to make up for the fact that it is called upon as a public institution to deal with traffic which is not profitable, but which is traffic which most Canadians insist on, with every right to do so.
I want to say to all colleagues that this party supports the bill. We think it represents a new beginning. Of course, we will be watching very carefully how the Post Office conducts its business affairs. I must say on behalf of my party we wish management and the employees of the Post Office well. We understand perfectly the immensity of the task which lies before them. My experience in dealing with the leaders of the unions in the Post Office has convinced me that the rank and file of Canada Post are as anxious to reform the Post Office and deliver the kind of service they expect Canadians to have as anyone else.
It is my very great privilege and pleasure to wish everyone in the Post Office well, with a sincere desire that the postal service of Canada improve and continue improving as the months and years go on.

The point I want to discuss this afternoon, and the subject of my amendment, is a rather narrow one. It deals with an amendment to tariff item 47810-1. The facts of the matter are these, Mr. Speaker. Prior to November 9, 1979, the Department of National Revenue collected duties on dental materials because it considered that the words "surgery" and "surgical prosthesis" in tariff item 47810-1 did not include dental surgery or dental surgical prosthesis. However, under appeal No. 1377 the Tariff Board ruled that the term "surgery" did include dental surgery and that "other surgical prosthesis" included dental prosthesis. The Tariff Board found that the customs administration had been in error for many years.
Customs Tariff
One might ask what happens to all that revenue which was apparently improperly collected. Has any of it been refunded? Is this merely one of those cases where the taxpayer has been told "tough luck"? In any event, that is not the subject matter of our discussion this afternoon.
The Tariff Board's ruling meant that no duties were payable in accordance with the law as it was written. However, the one firm in Canada engaged in a minor way in the manufacture of dental materials, that is Johnson and Johnson (Canada), wrote to the Department of Finance to have the duties introduced on amalgams and other dental materials at the levels which Customs had been collecting in error. While the dental laboratories conference did complain about the fact that duties would be removed from finished prosthesis, they did not ask that duties be imposed on dental materials. Indeed, when the conference determined that removal of duty-free treatment for dental prosthesis would mean the consequent elimination under tariff item 47900-1 of duty-free treatment for dental materials, they withdrew their request. The officials in the Department of Finance indicated, quite rightly, that the main petitioners for the restoration of the duty which had originally been collected in error were Johnson and Johnson. That is all this budget does, notwithstanding the fact that the Canadian Dental Association, on behalf of all Canadian dentists, is opposed to this particular proposal.
I have before me correspondence addressed to the minister from the president of the Canadian Dental Association, as well as to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) which gives some more background. The Canadian Dental Association was not consulted before changes to tariff item 47810-1 were proposed in the budget.
That is one point about which I believe the officials in finance are more than arrogant. I know that in the United States, for instance, industry, associations and all aspects of the economy have the opportunity to be consulted before a budget is actually taken up and passed. In England I know that associations, such as dental associations and other trade and manufacturing associations, are consulted before changes are made in legislation affecting the amount of duty and tariffs. And why not? Is this question of taxation a cat and mouse affair that the Minister of Finance springs like a hungry cat on some unsuspecting mice or other targets at the time of the budget so that he can wring from those particular bodies or individuals the maximum tax?
I would like to receive an answer from the minister as to why there was not consultation with the Canadian Dental Association and why the Department of Finance has chosen to plug the so-called loophole. It was a bad practice. It does not bring in any revenue. It does not do a darned thing. There are no dental supplies manufactured in Canada other than the limited amalgams put on the market by Johnson and Johnson, which I think back in 1974 bought a process which had been developed at the University of Alberta in Edmonton. The amalgams are manufactured here in limited amounts. They are manufactured much more in the United States, brought

April 14, 1981
Customs Tariff
into Canada in bulk and sold here. There are no other dental materials made in Canada, with the exception of some prosthesis; but that is not the point. There was no objection expressed by the conference on that question and no action taken by the government in the budget.
All I am saying is that these materials used in dental surgery shall not be subject to the Customs Tariff as provided for under tariff item 47810-1. It seems to me that all along there has been the strongest possible case-I will admit it is on a very narrow item-for the government to leave the matter alone. The government is not going to encourage the production of these amalgams or other materials in Canada. There is not the market for these products in Canada. One could almost apply a 25 per cent tariff against American products and they would still be purchased by Canadian supply houses and sold to Canadian dentists at a price lower than the manufacturing price, along with the normal taxes that would be imposed in Canada. We would naturally impose a 9 per cent sales tax on those items.
I suggest to the minister today, as I have privately, that this matter could easily be conceded by the government and there would be absolutely no measurable impact on revenues. That is not the question. It is the principle that officials were right. We will see that they were right even though they were judged to be wrong. That is the sole effect of the government trying to restore an interpretation to a tariff item which the Tariff Board said has been wrong for so many years. I urge hon. members to accept the amendment and we could then adopt the whole bill as amended.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), as he so aptly explained, is intended to strike out from Schedule VI of the bill a provision, or rather to make inoperative a provision contained in Schedule VI which bears tariff item No. 47810-1 and whose purpose is to reapply rates in force before an amendment made at about the end of 1970 and which came in 1979 after an interpretation of that tariff item by the Tariff Board. The effect of the new interpretation was to authorize the free entry of several dental materials which were subject to rates before that decision. Therefore, what we are doing in Schedule VI is to revert to the situation as it was before the board's decision.
Canadian production of certain of those goods such as dental obturation materials, had been started on the understanding that imports might not be duty-free. In addition, certain laboratories which manufacture dental prostheses realized that laboratories located in the United States were taking business away from them. With this provision we are therefore reverting to a previous situation, while taking into account the overall objective of a tariff policy designed to encourage the production in Canada of certain materials or certain merchandise or goods, in this instance those used in the production of dental prostheses.
However, in view of the numerous representations we have received since the budget was tabled about the complexity of the tariff provisions in the case of dental suppliers, Department of Finance officials have undertaken an in-depth study of the situation of all dental products to which rates are applicable. Unfortunately, it is now too early to announce the type of changes, if any, which might be proposed as a result of that study. It is also impossible to promise that everyone will be satisfied with the outcome of that study because, if we take a close look at the issue, we realize that there are very diverse interests between those who import such products and the Canadian manufacturers of the same merchandise and the same products.
Officials of the department are in consultation with commercial and professional dental associations. Other departments such as Industry, Trade and Commerce and National Health and Welfare will also be consulted in this in-depth study. I would also like to indicate, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian dentists have written to me to say that dental materials have increased 27 per cent. Now, reality does not seem to bear that out. The amendments contained in the budget affect only dental prostheses, materials and articles that are part of a finished prostheses as well as materials used in reconstructive dental surgery. The duty which is generally applied to these items is between 7 and \1'A per cent, although some still enter the country duty-free.
The instruments and other dental materials used by dentists are not at all affected by this change and I must add that most of these items, such as the materials, still come into the country duty-free. The items covered by the provision contained in Bill C-50 are in fact responsible for only a very small portion of total dental costs and would represent only a very small fraction of a possible future cost increase resulting from this amendment. I would think that possible increases will result from higher costs of materials used in dental prostheses, rather than from the changes resulting from Bill C-50.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, an in-depth study is under way and I think it is too early yet to agree to an amendment such as the one proposed by the hon. member. I would therefore suggest that the House reject the amendment put by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). However, I want to tell him and the House that his proposal is being given serious consideration, that the whole situation is being subjected to an in-depth and exhaustive review, and that we will be in a position to make a decision once this review is completed.

In passing, I would like to point out to the hon. member that the general purpose of the tariff policy is to allow the Canadian manufacturing industry a certain margin of action in the production of certain goods. This is precisely why we are reinstating this tariff, to allow the Canadian industry to enter this sector of production.
The hon. member is asking me why we do not wait. As I have already stated, there are diverse interests involved. Obviously, the interests of the importer are not the same as those of the producers of such materials, even though there might be very few of them. We also say that we must maintain this relative protection. And we have seen that the margin is still not too wide to provide a certain freedom of action for Canadian manufacturers. We are now reviewing this whole situation. We shall find out what is the position of the various interests, and when we have reviewed the situation, we shall make a decision. This does not mean that the decision will be to remove the tariff. It could very easily be to maintain it.
