Mr. Speaker, having seen some examples of how the government, having once levied a duty, will not let go, I want to speak about a little incident regarding some rather minor products that have a lot of contact with Canadians. I suppose there is hardly anyone who does not have some dental repair work or dental surgery done, so all of us will be affected by the decisions made by the government this afternoon.
I also have some doubts about the bona fides of those at the administrative level. I suppose that at some time or other all of us indulge in civil service or bureaucrat bashing. A lot of it is justified. I have been here for about 23 years and the longer I am here the more difficult I find it to fathom the mental process of the bureaucratic mind and the type of philosophy that permeates it. For many, it is that it will be right and right at all times, regardless of how wrong it may be. We have seen evidence of that in some of the practices of the revenue-gathering departments.
In the Department of Employment and Immigration we have seen bureaucracy become a law unto itself. The incident is merely a game; a practice which had been adjudged to be in error, even though an error of many years. I could not justify the minister's thinking when he said that it had been the government's intention or policy to subject the dental materials covered by item No. 47810-1 to customs duty. How can he tell us this? The words do not say so, because the Tariff Board says the words do not say so. There is no indication that that was the government's intention. It is the government's present intention, of course, that this should be covered, but to say that it was the intention when the tariff item was set up is to beg the question and, to me, is not justified by the events. But that is a minor item, Mr. Speaker.
Today we are on their reading of a bill that is as imposing in bulk as was the Bank Act. It covers a great deal of ground. The amendments to the Customs Tariff are detailed and laborious and there is nothing that is less interesting or more sterile for us to examine. These amendments arise out of the changes made at the Tokyo Round which is, in effect, a liberalization of tariff walls among trading partners. That is something that is welcomed on both sides of the House.
Some of these amendments will be of gradual tenure; they will be in effect over eight years subject, of course, to the sometimes wild flights of fancy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who feels that he can wrestle inflation to the ground by slashing prices in Canada to meet those of

April 14, 1981
Customs Tariff
imports and thus make Canadian producers become more competitive. Goodness knows how much this lengthy exercise has cost the Government of Canada or how much it has cost a number of provinces to send people to attend the negotiations in Tokyo and in Geneva. Trade associations also sent delegations to give testimony to the negotiators. The whole effort, which lasted a number of years, has cost us a great deal of time and effort but is a step in the right direction. In some ways it is the negation of economic nationalism. This economic nationalism moves around the world in various and often unexpected ways.
Let us consider the Common Market. The nine members dispense with tariff barriers between the partners. This does not dispense with tensions among the various competing producers of goods and services within the community, however. One should hear what the French say about the English. And Britain is taking a hard, second look at its membership in the Common Market. France is apprehensive about Spain coming in. Each is trying to protect its own interests and, of course, to sell more goods to its neighbour. The object is never to buy more but always to sell more.
Judging from outward appearances, one might think that the Common Market represented a decline in economic nationalism, but is that really so? The Italians send tanker after tanker of red wine into the Bordeaux region to be mixed with the French production. When the French farmers hear about this, the trucks are summarily dumped by the wayside. Truckloads of Italian tomatoes are dumped in France. French wine is dumped in Germany. Now they are talking about English mutton and lamb. Goodness, those poor little beasties are getting some great maledictions in France!
Although there is still tension, it is certainly a great deal less than the tension created by the economic nationalism which some of us, who in the 1930s were teenagers, saw rampant in Europe and in other parts of the world, including Canada and the United States, when tariff walls were raised out of sight, and everybody closed their doors. What did we get out of it? We got World War II. It was bound to come.
The implementation of Bill C-50,1 think, is a gesture on the part of Canada. I know it will receive assent on both sides as a stamp against economic nationalism. Through it, we are going to open up trade, which is the production and exchange of goods. True enough, that is not sufficient because Bill C-50 does nothing about non-tariff barriers. If there is anything which can get more oppressive and difficult to deal with, I would like to know what it is.
There are countries around the world which are great traders as long as their goods can be put in someone else's market. But try to get some of our goods, of a generally competitive nature, manufactured goods, for instance, into one of their markets. Try to get manufactured goods into Japan. There are all sorts of reasons why manufactured goods cannot appear on the Japanese market.
Let us deal now with the Common Market. Canada has heavy machinery plants, and in the pulp and paper manufacturing area as well as in the generation of electricity we have firms which stand second to none in the world. But it is very difficult for those firms to get tender documents not only from Common Market countries but also from Britain. The British board of trade simply says that there is nothing doing, that there are no copies of the tender documents available to anybody else, that the products in question will be made in Britain or within the Common Market. We are excluded. That non-tariff barrier is as good as slapping a 100 per cent customs tariff on the goods and services.
I do not think this House has had a satisfactory explanation from the ministers concerned as to what progress has been made, where further progress might be made, or to what practices Canada objects. Nor have we been told who are the greatest offenders regarding non-tariff barriers. I know we have some. If such be the case, let our trading partners tell us. I understand that some of our European friends consider our anti-dumping rules to be pretty barbarous. On the other hand, I invite the Europeans to look at some of their own. We can look at our American friends and see what they do. Some of their treasury board rulings and designations could be said to be pretty fast and vicious. We have only to look at some examples.
I always say try to sell ideas and commodities. We should not dwell on the difficulties. Let us see how we can do things. We should always stress everything positively. Do not tell me how you cannot do something, Mr. Speaker; I want to know how you are going to do it. I think that is how we should approach our negotiations. We should not put emphasis on the difficulties. I am not suggesting that our negotiators, in this particular round leading up to the accord embodied in Bill C-50, took that approach. They had a difficult task. The only thing many of us would reproach them for is their absolute secrecy in the early days. Everything was close to their chest at that time. They would not approach provincial governments. Literally they had to be dragged kicking and screaming into co-operation with the provinces. They would not take industry into their confidence. Things were very very difficult.
I think this is because there is a mental block in the bureaucracy in Canada that does not want to talk to business openly. There is a wall. Maybe it is the old Chinese wall. Nevertheless, a barricade exists between Canadian industry and what is known as government service. I would not say it is deliberate or that able administrators here in Ottawa do it so they can run the show. I will not impute those motives to them. With notable exceptions, there does not seem to be the required relationship between Canadian industry, Canadian business and government circles in Ottawa. I shall not speak about the provincial capitals because I know nothing about their inner workings.
Having dealt with that background, by this bill we are going to put and end to the Union of South Africa Trade Agreement Act, 1932, the United Kingdom Trade Agreement Act, 1937, and the Irish Free State Trade Agreement Act, 1932. The
April 14, 1981

1932 acts are, of course, in line with the general treaty of that year arising out of the conference held in Ottawa which gave rise to the BP classification in our tariffs. It worked wonderfully well. As a matter of fact, if it had not been for the BP, a great deal of industry would not have been built in this country.
As a result of the British trade agreement and the preferential treatment, American firms established many manufacturing subsidiaries in Canada so they could hit the European and British market. Via the British market they were able to trade with Egypt, India, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, all the colonies and East Africa. It was, in fact, the old British Empire that gave birth 50 years ago to the development of a great deal of Canadian industry.
This has created a branch plant economy in many industries. However, that is the only way there is going to be any industry. When the 1932 agreements were negotiated and implemented, this country had a remarkably small population of 11 million and had to deal with 50 million people in Britain, 50 million in France, 60 million or more in Germany, as well as the populations of Japan, China, India and the rest of the world. We were one little pea in a big bag of little peas and some big ones.
To put it in balance, we must be grateful for those men in the various countries who in 1931 and 1932 negotiated British preferential treatment, the British Trade Agreement Act and the various acts we are now repealing 50 years later. The reason is that Britain, having gone through the turmoil of World War II and a generation of terrible troubles thereafter, joined the Common Market, as did Ireland. We are totally excluded. It is meaningless to have British preferential treatment when Britain and Ireland are members of the Common Market.
In so far as South Africa is concerned, it too was a member of the group in 1932. It has gone its divergent way and is now being ostracized by countries in the rest of the world, many of whom are the world's greatest hypocrites. That is not the way to treat the troubles in South Africa. I certainly do not like apartheid, but we practise it here in Canada, only with more subtlety and with greater hypocrisy.
I find it absolutely unjustifiable that we have Canadian churchmen and various groups belabouring South Africa. I say physician cure thyself before you start preaching about others. Nevertheless, we are putting an end to our trade with South Africa on a preferential basis. I regret it. I think of all we could have done with South Africa. By being friends and maintaining communications with them, we could perhaps convince them to amend their ways and they could convince us to amend ours. By placing them in a ghetto and ostracizing them, we will not gain any influence over them, not if I know the people of South Africa, and I met many of them during World War II and have known others since that time. However, such has been the way of public thinking and the actions of government, because it was the popular thing to do.
Customs Tariff
We have put an end to our trade agreement with South Africa and put their goods under the general tariff. That will not change anything in South Africa one iota. What we have done shows the narrowness of our minds. Some day we will regret it. In Rhodesia we participated in an action against people who have now had to turn over government to elements whose future can be contemplated with some concern.
The whole of the continent of Africa is close to domination by the Soviet Union. It is being delivered. With patience, in ten to 15 years the Soviet Union will get the whole of North Africa. Next, of course, will be South Africa. That is the only bastion. When that happens, the United States will rue the day of their Andrew Youngs and others who ran about opening up the defences against the Soviet Union. These comments do not relate to this bill, but I hope the House will excuse my discursive remarks because they do relate to South Africa. Perhaps I can get a reaction from some members in this House. As soon as I mention South Africa, some of them tend to want to spit. I suggest they look at themselves in the mirror to see whether they should not spit at themselves.
I had a minor difference of opinion with the minister on one particular point. However, I recommend that the House pass Bill C-50. In saying that, the Minister of State for Finance is the jack-of-all-trades in finance. He is handling this Customs Tariff bill. From where is the initiative to come for other changes? Where are some real initiatives with regard to non-tariff barriers? Will we have to get at non-tariff barriers by tackling them through our participation in international financial organizations? One area I suggest to the minister we might investigate in order possibly to get at some of these artificial barriers is the Inter American Development Bank. Our participation in that concern is at a reasonable level. Along with our friends in the United States, we carry a considerable wallop.
If various developing countries approach Canada, the United States and others with regard to financial aid on a multilateral basis, we should make it conditional upon the removal of certain improper trade practices to which we feel we are subject.
After all, if the United States can tie some of its economic relations and its economic help to human rights, there is no reason why we could not tie some economic aid to the removal of certain barriers. I offer the suggestion. Through the World Bank we participate in financial assistance in the Far East. There may be some bilateral financial assistance. However, this is where it becomes practical. That is our chief obstacle to increasing Canadian trade, apart from our high cost of production and, I think, perhaps a great deal of lack of interest on the part of Canadian businessmen who will not get out and really hack it on the market. Our Canadian banks are available for financing. The Export Development Corporation is there work-

Mr. Speaker, 1 do not intend to take a great deal of time in dealing with this bill but 1 do want to make some comments. The last comment of the previous speaker was of considerable interest to me. I think he is right that we have to get a better understanding of the imposition of non-tariff barriers as they come into play and into force, while on the other hand we are seeing a move by these very same countries to support the reduction, gradual or otherwise, of existing tariffs.
I know the minister's department has looked at this matter, and I am sure in times gone by the House of Commons has also looked at the impact of tariffs and the effect they have both on domestic industry and on its capacity to exist, but before I deal with that I want to say that on the matter of South Africa I noted that my colleague from the Conservative Party was waxing eloquent just a few moments ago. I think he must surely understand that every measure must be used during periods of time when it is generally acknowledged by the administration itself and by others around the world that the policies enacted by an administration toward people create situations which are discriminatory and which are considered by the majority in the free world to be unsatisfactory or unconscionable.
I therefore do not want to engage in a discussion of the relative merits of the hon. member's argument other than to say that the same argument can and has been used about other countries over many years, and there comes a point in time when an action is appropriate. At the time the actions taken were deemed to be appropriate, and I think they were appropriate.
Let me turn to the bill and the general philosophy of the bill. My concern is that as we see the nations of the world, Canada being one of them, galloping along toward free trade, the impact of that movement on Canadian manufacturing, Canadian exporting and the capacity of Canada to hold its place in the world and to provide employment opportunities and economic opportunities for Canadians in this country becomes somewhat suspect. I am sure I do not have to go back into history to explain the historic significance of tariff barriers. Much of the industry which exists in Canada, and has for 50, 60 or more years, is of a branch plant nature. It came to Canada in order to get behind the tariff wall. I think before we move too swiftly toward the elimination of tariffs, we have to appreciate that our situation is somewhat different from those of a number of other countries.
The movement away from a tariff wall, so to speak, toward a free trade, though it may be of benefit to certain areas of industry, could be disastrous for other areas. We must fully
understand the branch-plant nature of Canada's economy. The reason why the branch-plant was set up in Canada was to make available an operation which would be able to take advantage of the domestic Canadian market while at the same time not having to pay the tariff which would have raised the product above the price that would have been the price established for the Canadian manufacturer.
Canadian industry is small. Generally speaking, it meets a market of about 10 per cent of the U.S. market. Our major trading partner is the U.S. Most of the branch-plant nature of Canada's industry is related directly to the United States. The U.S. manufacturing capacity is large enough so that if it had the desire and if there were no impediments in the way, it could quite conceivably meet the entire Canadian market requirements out of its current unused productive capacity. But it is not unreasonable to think that much of the nine million household requirements in Canada could easily be met by the indigenous capacity of U.S. industry to manufacture that is not currently being utilized.
If we were to have a free trade arrangement, as has been proposed by a committee of the other place-or at least is being considered by a committee of the other place-or if we were to go too swiftly toward free trade, there would be no imperative reason for the parent company to put the necessary capital reinvestment into the Canadian operation to maintain its efficiency. The end result of that could and, I suggest, would be that the Canadian operation would be allowed for a time to continue to operate, but in the final analysis it would not be kept competitive with its parent within the U.S. and in the end would become redundant. The justification would be that it should be closed because it is no longer competitive, and the U.S. manufacturer would solidify all of his manufacturing in his home base and would then just simply ship his products to Canada as manufacturers ship from Oregon to California, from Ohio to Florida or from West Virginia to South Carolina. That would be the relationship.
One of the factors we have going for us in regard to standing in the way is that we have a reasonably large domestic market, but not large enough to sustain if there is no reason for maintaining the efficiency of the industry. I think we have seen in the auto industry the very thing I am talking about. The auto industry is a rationalized North American industry. It is faced with a downturn in its market as a result, in many instances, of inefficient management unable to foresee what was evident to other manufacturers, and the initial reaction of the industry was to attempt to rebuild its industry within its home base, the United States, and to put less of its reinvestment dollars into Canada. It was only because we were able to say that at some point, I suppose, we could return to a tariff arrangement-and we did have in place some kind of agreement-that we were able to keep the industry from centralizing its operations almost totally in Michigan or in other parts of the northern and mid-northern United States.
April 14, 1981

I am frankly concerned that we are moving with some haste to establish a free trade arrangement over a period of time that will work to the detriment of Canadian industry, because of its branch-plant nature, that will work therefore to the detriment of Canadians in general, will not result in lower prices as many people anticipate it will, but will, in the final analysis, because of the lack of competition in Canada, result ultimately in higher prices because we will have to buy many, if not all, the products we want from offshore.
Without engaging in a long and difficult argument, I want to suggest that all is not quite as cut and dried as the provisions of this bill and the suggestions made by other people would make it appear to be. There is a requirement from the Canadian public on the Canadian Parliament to have a better understanding of the possible and likely implications of this move. Although consumer groups, and I support them in many things, may feel at first glance there is significant benefit to Canadian consumers by a reduction in tariff, because they will be able to gain access to what are today cheaper goods, the only thing which makes those goods cheaper is the fact that they have to compete with a Canadian-made product. Witness the soft fruit industry. Those of you who are familiar with the soft fruit growers' industry can appreciate the difficulty that industry has had over the years in competing with the influx of soft fruit grown in the United States and in other parts of the world, and the access that soft fruit has to the Canadian marketplace. You will appreciate the problems of the farmer who is faced with having to attempt to make ends meet with what is the mean average of the mid and end-of-season price while the importer is able to take advantage of the early, mid and end-season price and, therefore, has a much higher mean average. He is therefore able, because of climatic conditions and access to the Canadian market, to force the Canadian farmer in that industry at least-I am not familiar with other farming groups, but my colleague may be able to speak to them-to become competitive with considerably less cash flow and, therefore, a smaller profit margin. I am familiar with this group representing an area that was substantially involved. The Canadian farmer in that particular industry, in Ontario at least and in other parts of the country, is faced with this problem.
I want you to extrapolate that, if you will, and position yourselves in relation to a number of other industry sectors, considering the impact of allowing that which is happening in the farming industry to occur in those other industry sectors. If there were no tariffs in place, and if there was no reason, other than the marketplace, to want to be located in Canada for manufacturing purposes, then it is not unreasonable to assume that many of what are now called the North American multinational giants, but what really are U.S. multinational giants, would find no good or justifiable reason for maintaining their employment levels, plants or efficiency here.
My recommendation in this regard is, first of all, that we approach it with caution, and second, that we structure here in the House of Commons a group which will once again take a
Customs Tariff
serious and hard look at the ever-changing nature, particularly now, of Canada's economic base. We should look at the winners and losers and the reasons there are those winners and losers in Canada's manufacturing sector. We should try to understand through an analysis the reasons why there have been so many plant closures in Canada in the last 24 to 48 months. We should determine whether those plant closures resulted simply from a rationalization of the parent operations in respect of greater productivity, and determine whether the increasing and potential opening of the market of Canada to a free trade arrangement will not be in the long run more of a hazard than a help to us.
There are certain specific groups we all hear from, ranging from the shirt manufacturers, who have written, I am sure, to each and every one of us, to the dental associations which have written to us on the other side of the issue, which are making a very valid case that has to be given careful consideration. But the basic and more fundamental problem is one that we will face somewhere down the road. My view of it, having had discussions of late with people in the United States and having looked at the potential hazard to the Canadian manufacturing sector in particular, is that if we were to move with unseemly haste, we could well create a situation which would allow them, quite justifiably, to say they need no longer be located here. The end result of that, of course, could be quite disastrous. It would require us to become even more dependent on our raw materials in order to maintain our standard of living. It would require us to sell ever more of those materials in an unprocessed and semi-processed state in order to maintain that standard of living. The political pressures to continue the wholesale sale of our basic heritage would be immense, and it is questionable whether any government, Liberal, Conservative or NDP, regardless of where it was located in the country, would be able to withstand those pressures, given the unemployment and the lack of economic opportunity which would become the order of the day.
I do not pretend for a moment to be an expert in the field, although I have studied it at some length for many years, and I do not know when you ever become an expert because experts seem to have very conflicting opinions, but having looked at it, I see some indications of potential difficulties. In our desire to appear to be nice guys in the world of trade and commerce, we are not only agreeing to reductions in and elimination of tariffs, we do not even understand that the countries with which we agree, or with which we enter into these agreements, do not necessarily always live up to the letter of the agreements.
Those of us who have looked at the problem still have a long and somewhat curious view of the DISC program in the United States, for example, and the fact that it was found, I think it is fair to say, to be outside the GATT Agreement. That did not end it. It stayed in place, nevertheless, because it would seem to be of some national concern and some national benefit. There are few of us who do not understand that in Japan, particularly in the automobile field, while there may well be a willingness to reduce the tariff, the possibility of

entering the market as a result of all the other non-tariff barriers which are placed before the sale can be consummated is virtually non-existent for the North American manufacturer.
It concerns me when I hear people cheering about the reduction in anti-pollution control measures and safety measures in the United States. They seem to indicate that it is of some benefit to the industry at a time when industries are spending considerable sums of money re-tooling for world production. Many of the countries to which these companies hope to sell will demand that those anti-pollution devices and safety measures, which the United States is prepared to set aside for now, be in place. So, the cost will be considerably higher to produce two different levels of automobiles. They did not stick to their guns in an attempt to produce one automobile which met the world demand. Rather, they succumbed to pressures of a domestic kind.
Very few people recognize that one of the reasons we have difficulty selling aircraft in Japan is that the country is currently in the business of developing an aircraft industry. While they would argue, on the one hand, that they do not have tariffs to make it difficult for anyone to sell, on the other hand, by virtue of other measures, they make it impossible to sell.
If I may say so, we must put aside our boy scout attitude. I do not mean this in any derogatory sense, but the fact is that the world operates in a very tough-minded way. Therefore, countries of the world make their decisions based on what is in their best interests. The direction in which we are travelling may not be in our best interest. We may not be exercising the care and caution which is required to safeguard the industrial opportunity of Canada for future generations.
The whole area is fraught with question marks. The minister has entered into and completed the negotiations. He should know that what is on paper does not necessarily always reflect what one meets in the marketplace when one tries to do business in other countries. That is why I think the comment of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was correct. We must get a handle on the non-tariff barrier problems which exist around the world and their effect on our enterprises which are attempting to do business outside Canada. We must get a handle on the extent to which the branch-plant nature of our economy is influenced by the parent operation and on the real possibility that free access to our marketplace could undermine the necessary investment to maintain the competitive position we require if we are to provide for ourselves.
We need a much more thorough review of the situation. We should look at today's society instead of adopting the ten-year-old view of the situation. We must look at the ever-changing economic conditions in every part of the world and the difficulties with which the manufacturing sector is faced.
We will not delay this legislation unduly today, but I hope the minister will be able to make a commitment that in the
near future he will establish a group compromised of members of the House of Commons to look at the very difficult problems about which everyone talks but which no one really understands.
How do we enter the Japanese market? It is not a matter of building a better mouse trap. If we build a better mouse trap, they will keep us out until they have built a better one still. Anyone who is knowledgeable about international trade understands that. Therefore, when we take a look at Japan in the context of the rest of the world which is pooling its resources to solidify its economic conditions, it chills our spines, especially when we think of what might happen in the future.
I ask the minister to give these suggestions some thought before we are much further down the road. There may be a point beyond which we cannot possibly return. The minister must realize that countries do not necessarily operate by the written rules; they operate by the ones which serve them best.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make three brief comments in connection with the impact of tariffs. Canada is a vast and diversified country. In my view we must give a lot of consideration, when we set or remove tariffs, to the impact this will have on every part of our country. For instance, at the present time there is a rather heavy tariff on logs coming from the United States into western Canada. This has made the building of log houses uncompetitive with other types of construction. It is having an adverse affect. Whoever set these tariffs should look at what they are doing to the housing industry in western Canada; I am sure they will realize then that some changes should be made.
My second comment is on the way in which items are handled. There are emergency organizations that deal with items that come into the country. Some tariff officials take too long to consider these things. There has been an arrangement for several years whereby some of these items, particularly in terms of landed or stalled aircraft, would go through immediately as an emergency. Recently there have been delays in the Calgary office. This could very well put a company out of business. With the current unemployment situation in Canada, we should encourage every industry to stay in business as well as bring in more business. Administrative delays in the handling of a piece of machinery for a stalled aeroplane could very well ruin a business.
Third, I think we should look at the impact of tariffs on all parts of the country: the "far east", central Canada and the west. Too often tariffs are set to accommodate only one part of the country. Western people today are paying much higher prices for clothes and shoes because of tariffs. We must protect our Canadian industries. On the other hand, the coal industries in the east and in the west have been downgraded because we have permitted American coal to come into the country without being subject to tariffs. Westerners pay more for shoes and clothes; but our miners are not working. We should consider the impact right across the country so that all Canadians receive the benefit of tariffs or no tariffs, whichever the case might be.
April 14, 1981

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This is the third time I have taken the floor today, on various subjects. We are now studying a bill from the Senate. Unfortunately we do not see that often enough because the subject we will debate this evening is indeed a good one for prior consideration by the Senate.
I for one have been convinced for years that unfortunately the government sets far too many bills aside for first consideration by the House of Commons; they could be sent to the Senate first because our colleagues there have a wide experience in government affairs and they could very well study them at a more leisurely pace and I would say under much less pressure.
Tax Conventions
I am not a leader of the official opposition, but on the other hand I do have a certain knowledge as a result of my experience in the House of Commons. As it happened I was debating Bill C-57 this afternoon, the excise tax measure. It is well known that I am the expert on excise matters on this side of the House. Later on in the afternoon the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Bussieres) brought in Bill C-50 for the consideration of the House. They rushed to come and get me because I had introduced amendments to Bill C-50 and if we are to study a bill having to do with double taxation I can say that, thanks to my experience, I am the expert on the Income Tax Act.
So here I am again tonight, for the third time. I apologize. I see the minister whom I know very well, but we are debating related but different subjects. Well, on this point I will speak at length. Although a Senate bill may look harmless and even if the subject may not seem very important either, it has to do with conventions to avoid double taxation so we are going to discuss the principles.
Mr. Minister, if I may, I would like to execute or rather to prod the goats behind you that are ruminating and seem to have only a ruminating interest in some of the comments made here.
It is just like what happened this afternoon when we were debating Bill C-57. During our discussions with the witnesses, certain government members were very excited and had animated exchanges with them. However, when we discussed the same bill this afternoon, they remained completely silent in the House, and those who were the most militant said that they were abstaining from the debate. Come on! Where is their political courage? Where is their moral courage? All I am asking them is to show some moral courage!
For my part, I must express my views on these bills. The government members can remain silent. They can take part in the committee proceedings in turns because they have a rotation system. I am thinking about the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, about the government members, about what happened when the committee was considering Bill C-57. I had to recognize about two dozen members who were there to represent the government. They are nothing but big lumps! Only a few of them are interested in the subject.
What I find most surprising is that they will then ask me: "Mr. Lambert, you are an expert in the matter. What is your opinion?" Well, I can say quite simply that it is not by being a big lump in committee that I became an expert.
I was a government member myself and I could reply to some parliamentarians who are now laughing up their sleeve that I was a parliamentary secretary myself long before them and much earlier in my career. I was also Speaker of the House and minister. They could start with that.
However, some bills are considered in committee, it is not enough to look clever in the House and gather around the

April 14, 1981
Tax Conventions
speakers to applaud them, because we now have television in the House and government members feel that they should gather around the member who is speaking.
I simply say to you, and the minister will admit it this evening, that one has to be familiar with the bill not only in committee but also in the House. Then the minister will be able to assess his colleagues as well as the members opposite. At present, after 24 years in the House of Commons, I think that I am rated quite low as far as ability is concerned. There are several bills with which I am familiar, such as the Income Tax Act, the Customs Act, the Excise Tax Act, and the Bank Act. I feel that I rank in the lower quarter. That does not mean that I do not consider myself ahead of the vast majority of my colleagues in this area.
But let us get back to the subject. We are considering tonight a convention to avoid double taxation with respect to income tax and to promote economic activity in either Canada, Australia or New Zealand. I must tell the minister that I have some reservations because, and bear with me in my philosophical reflections tonight after my lecture this afternoon, I think we as Canadians have not done our duty in view of the declining role played by the United Kingdom in the Commonwealth. It was up to us to show leadership in the Commonwealth. Yet, what have we done? We sat on our royal assets. Lack of interest! I have had ample opportunity in the last two decades to visit New Zealand and Australia and I knew their soldiers as prisoners of war in the 1940s. I had friends everywhere, in government, in the bureaucracy, that is in the public service, and among the people too. When I went to New Zealand, my arrival was simply announced and people everywhere knew me. The same thing happened in Australia, which I visited on several occasions. Do you know what our colleagues in those countries were blaming us for? They felt that we, as Canadians, were too aloof.
We were too hoity-toity. We were too concerned with our place in the North American Sun. We did not, Mr. Speaker, take up the challenge that the Australians and the New Zealanders wanted us to, not to dominate them, but to join them. I say this is the best we can do with Australia and New Zealand, that is to join them in the activities of the Commonwealth out in in the eastern Pacific. We are not going to dominate them. O Lord, the average Aussie would hit you over the head, and with justification, if you tried it. However, we should join them.
The United States has met with some problems out in the Pacific. We are not going to try to take advantage of them. However, Britain was caught up in some real problems in the 20 post-war years. We could have served the cause of the Commonwealth a great deal more, and here I am not going to attribute blame to any administration. It started from the time I was in Parliament. There was the most amazing silence and lack of co-operation. There was the feeling that the Aussies
and the New Zealanders were part of the Antarctic penguin group. It was almost that bad. In trying to accomplish certain problems within the Commonwealth, we have taken an attitude difficult to put into words. Frankly, I am disgusted with our attitudes on external affairs and defence. I used to be fairly close to that from 1963 until 1967, and even in the earlier years. However, I am amazed at our performance. This lackadaisical performance, this drifting with regard to the commonwealth, this drifting with regard to Australia and New Zealand has been more than countenanced by the present administration. All along their members have not cared one damn hoot. Why is that? I suppose it is because a lot of them felt that they were not part of World War II and therefore, in the spirit of a new generation, they felt that World War II was something that should be left in the past. They are like the kids who drifted on the streets in the 1960s and who said that the vets of the 1940s were part of history and should be forgotten, not one of them remembering that they sprung from the loins of a World War II vet and that life had been made safe for them as a result of the sacrifices of those who had ventured into the ranks of the armed services of the allies in the 1940s.
I am amazed at the complacent attitude that many people today hold toward people of my generation. We had a great deal to lose but we walked into the recruiting centres on a Saturday afternoon, we left universities in mid-course without thinking about any real challenge, but we were going to do our duty by our country. A good number of members on both sides of the House did that. I did it but I do not wear a medal on my arm and I would not care to. I will be damned, however, if I will be told by anybody in this House that I am less than loyal to this country because I oppose certain changes to the Constitution or because I oppose certain changes to the way of life that I defended.

Be that as it may, I want to come back to this particular bill and our relations with the Australians and the New Zealanders. To a whole generation, which encompasses the majority of government members, relationships with Australia and New Zealand are as strange as night is unto day. Few of them know Australians and fewer still know New Zealanders. We have missed the boat, Mr. Speaker. The opportunity was there. I knew the Aussies and I knew the New Zealanders and I know that year after year we have neglected our relationships with them. There could be formidable relationships today in trade and influence-influence at the United Nations and through working together. I am sure that if you had put together the Aussies, the Canadians and the New Zealanders, they would be marching as a team of three on the principles of the United Nations. Do they do that now? Not at all. We have been kept dispersed. I simply say that it is the responsibility of the administration that there has been this difficulty.
That we should have tax agreements with them is all to the good. Canadian oil drilling companies have headed out to Australia as the result of the National Energy Program. Other people are going to New Zealand to provide expertise. Ten or 12 years ago I remember that the husband of the president of the women's organization in my constituency was named by the government of New Zealand to head the offshore drilling program of the government of New Zealand. He was a Canadian who had acquired the expertise through working for one of the so-called international companies and because of personal relationships, was named to head the program.
This is the sort of contact that must be maintained between governments. When you know the people concerned and what they will be doing, you can help them and they can help you. The way some governments behave, you would almost think that some of our allies were enemies.
Turning to the detail of this particular bill, Mr. Speaker, there is one feature on which I should like some explanation and reassurance from the minister, and that is with regard to the changes that may be implemented in the agreements, that these shall be presented by way of resolution which shall be subject to affirmation by the House, if I am correct.
There are many other parts to this bill. I invite the hon. member who sits behind the minister and says "read the bill," to read the government fact sheet. He has not seen it, obviously. I will elucidate what this bill covers because the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) who made that statement obviously is not aware of what is in this bill.
What are the specific provisions of this tax treaty? First, witholding tax; second, capital gains; third, non-discrimination; fourth, teachers. Incidentally, there is no specific provision for teachers. Next come the provisions governing pensions and annuities. There are no tax hideaways for pensioners. You cannot decide that you are going to live in some of the more salubrious lands of Australia or New Zealand hoping to live in
Tax Conventions
a tax hideaway. Next we find relief from double taxation and the anticipated legislative timetable. This bill was supposed to be referred to the Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce in the Senate. Next we find the anticipated nature of the reaction to the tax treaties. The bill is unlikely to be opposed, it says in this release. We can question some of it in so far as points of discussion are concerned. This is a government handout. The parliamentary secretary would have been as entitled to it as I have, but I got it. He did not.
In so far as New Zealand is concerned, the question might be asked how the new treaty differs from the existing 1948 agreement. The main differences are the following: first, witholding tax, and second, dividends.
Article 10 of the treaty provides that dividends paid to residents of one country by a company which is a resident of the other country may be taxed at the source country at a maximum rate of 15 per cent. There was no such limitation in the 1948 agreement.
Article 11 covers interest. It provides for a general rate of tax of 15 per cent in the source country. There were no such limitations under the 1948 agreement.
Article 12 covers royalties. It provides for a general tax rate of 15 per cent in the source country. The 1948 agreement provides for an exemption in the case of copyright royalty but does not put a ceiling on other royalties. I am sure the parliamentary secretary was fully aware of this.
In the case of capital gains, the rules under Article 13 permit a country to tax capital gains realized on the disposition of real property and of rights to exploit or to explore for natural resources found in that country. They do not restrict the domestic rules. I am sure the parliamentary secretary is able to explain all of these applications. The 1948 agreement does not deal with the taxation of capital gains. After all, the capital gains tax did not exist in Canada at that time. Therefore, the respective domestic rules are applicable.
What about non-discrimination? The revised treaty rights of the 1948 agreement do not contain any specific rules on non-discrimination.
Here is something for the parliamentary secretary for I am sure he will be interested in pensions and annuities. Under the 1948 agreement, pensions and annuities are taxable only in the country where the recipient resides. Article 17 of the revised treaty does not reflect that policy. It recognizes the right of either country to tax such payments at source provided they exceed $10,000. It is hoped the parliamentary secretary will serve in this House long enough to qualify for a pension in excess of $10,000. Then he might branch out to find out just what Australia and New Zealand have to say about the taxation of pension payments.
In so far as teachers are concerned, the two-year tax exemption provided visiting teachers in the 1948 agreement will be terminated. This is something of great interest, particularly in western Canada.

Tax Conventions
With reference to Australia, the question might also be asked as to how the new treaty differs from the 1957 agreement. The main differences are the following; first, withholding tax on dividends. Article 10 of the treaty provides that dividends paid to residents of one country by a company which is a resident of the other country may be taxed in the source country at a maximum rate of 15 per cent. This is of some benefit. The 1957 agreement also provides for a 15 per cent limitation. Article 11 covers interest. It provides for a general rate of tax of 15 per cent in the source country. There are no limitations under the 1957 agreement. Article 12 covers royalties. It provides for a general tax rate of 10 per cent in the source country. The 1957 agreement provides for an exemption in the case of copyright royalties but has not put a ceiling on other royalties.
Considering the attitude of the Government of Canada with regard to royalties, we hope many Australians have invested in Canadian oil lands because they will only receive 10 per cent on royalties. That does not mean that the Government of Canada will not raid Canadian owners of royalties on oil lands because the government has already indicated its disposition to depredation.
The rules in Article 13 provide that a country may tax capital gains realized on disposition of real property and of rights to exploit or to explore for natural resources found in that country. They do not restrict domestic rules. The 1957 agreement does not deal with the taxation of capital gains. Therefore, the respective domestic rules are applicable. See if you can sort that out within the Canadian and Australian taxation rules.
The revised treaty does not contain any specific rules on non-discrimination. In so far as pensions and annuities are concerned, under the 1957 agreement pensions and annuities are taxable only in the country where the recipient resides. Article 18 of the revised treaty does not reflect that policy. It recognizes the right of either country to tax such payments at source.
As I recall it, minister Benson, standing in this House at the time of the so-called revision of the Income Tax Act, said that it was Canada's right and obligation to tax all pensions at 25 per cent, regardless of where the recipient resided and how that recipient had earned his pension. I presume that is the situation in Canada. Therefore, that is also the situation in Australia and New Zealand where the pension of any Canadian who qualifies will be taxed at the same 25 per cent base rate.
In so far as teachers in Australia are concerned, the two-year tax exemption provided visiting teachers in the 1957 agreement will be terminated.
These are some of the factors with regard to this particular scheme. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will recall the particular difficulties we had with the former minister of justice, who was subsequently the minister of finance, Mr. John Turner, about amendments to agreements of this size which shall be subject to either positive or negative resolutions of this House. If there has been one
subject about which there has been lengthy discussion in this House, one which has lasted now for 16 or 17 years, it is precisely that question of how to act in accordance with the rules. This is a reflection on House leadership. Frankly, they were scared-I was going to use a more awkward word-to refer the House rules to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization and request that it bring forward modernized rules reflecting the views of both sides of the House after what can only be qualified as a dog's breakfast which was imposed on this House in 1969. We knew it was a dog's breakfast but the government did not. Now we hear all sorts of comments about the House rules from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others about how they are abused. They fashioned the rules, let them live by them.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and other members, including some on the government side, who were interested in the rules at that time reached a consensus on how the matter should be handled throught the rules rather than through statutes. We have about half a dozen statutes kicking around in various places which determine how this House will act upon affirmative or negative resolutions for the purpose of bringing forward orders in council which may amend certain statutes. We have them in tax statutes with regard to double taxation. We have them with regard to the revision of statutory instruments. Now we are introducing them into the double taxation statute which is before us this evening.
The situation is less than a dog's breakfast. It requires a little good will on the part of the government. The government should say that it will consider the question of affirmativenegative resolutions with regard to orders in council affecting legislation or changes to certain legislation, and amend them to comply with the rules of the House so they do not depend upon erratic statutes that live here, there and about.
Government House leaders have been scared stiff. At the beginning of this session, the present government House leader was thumping loudly on his desk, speaking ad nauseam over the television about the changes that would have to be brought into this House in order to bring the rules up to date. I remember when he was a freshman member on the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. What he says today has not changed one iota from what he said then when he did not know which end was up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to follow my colleague for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who is much more knowledgeable than I with respect to income tax bills and tax treaties.
I compliment the government on reorganizing the tax treaty between Canada and New Zealand. I am surprised it took so long to produce a new tax treaty following the amendments to the Income Tax Act of 1971. It is high time the government managed to get this treaty organized. It was given first reading in the Senate in 1980, nine years late. In fact, at this point it is ten years late.
This should have been done at the time of the income tax revisions because our trade with Australia and New Zealand is exceptionally important to this country. These countries have economies that are similar to that of Canada. Therefore, we should be doing a great deal more than at present.
I suggest the minister take to cabinet the suggestion at present being worked out and work on it a little harder, namely organize some kind of free trade treaty with Australia and New Zealand. Those countries are in the southern hemisphere. They have a standard of living which is to some extent comparable to ours, though perhaps not as high. These countries have the same kind of industrial and sociological base as Canada. They represent a total population in excess of 17 million. If it were combined with ours, we would have a free market of 40 million people, producers and consumers. It would make us more competitive and give us the production runs needed by our manufacturing industry.
Goods manufactured in those countries could be sold in this country off season, and our goods could be sold in Australia and New Zealand also off season. That would give all three countries an opportunity to extend the length of production runs and would make it possible for us all to take part in the kind of industrial activity which is so important.
This is why tax treaties are important. It makes it possible for entrepreneurs in Canada to set up business in Australia and New Zealand and not be penalized by taxes. In the same way, entrepreneurs in New Zealand and Australia can set up operations in Canada without being penalized. That is the essential point in trade negotiations. An entrepreneur trying to do business in another country should not be double taxed.
I say to the minister that this is the first step, but only the first step. It is important that we organize the trade treaty, including taxation measures, so as to make it possible for us to integrate our markets. We in Canada have a market of only 24 million people, and we badly need a reciprocal market. We could have such a market with 41 million consumers if we joined Australia and New Zealand.
There has been some concern about imports into Canada of
meat products, fruit products and so forth from Australia, and
to some extent we tend to be parochial in that regard. The
Tax Conventions
truth of the matter is that when we have the same products for sale to the world, there is no reason why we cannot combine and organize our sales to the world in an effective manner to protect both our interests. If we had some sense, we would not be complaining about Australian beef, Australian lamb or Australian fruit. We would be getting together with both Australia and New Zealand to market through a central strategy meat, fruit, wheat, coal and nickel to the rest of the consuming world. We would not have to worry that they might sell some fruit in our market or they might sell some lamb or some beef in our market, or that we might sell our products in their market. What we would be doing as producers and suppliers is dealing as effectively with other countries as countries in the Middle East are dealing with us as suppliers of oil products.
It is about time we had a government which was prepared to look at this situation in a cold, businesslike sense and not just from the point of view of a simple tax treaty. We have made tax treaties with such countries as Malaysia and Singapore, but we should look at this from a sensible point of view. Australia and New Zealand could be our closest and best trading partners. Indeed, there should be a free trade arrangement and a free tax arrangement so that it would be clear that the tax on businesses in one country would not be doubled in another country. It is very important that we do this.
In presenting this legislation will the government, before this year is finished, complete the present negotiations with Australia and New Zealand, and will it go one step further by developing one common market for our countries?

Still, Clause 8 must be read followed by Clause 9 which stipulates that when an order under section 8 is used, it must be laid before Parliament and does not come into force until the thirtieth sitting day following its tabling, so that between the day it is tabled and that thirtieth sitting day, there is the possibility of addressing a motion to one or the other of the two Houses of Parliament with a view to cancelling the order, and that said motion must be signed by 50 hon. members.
So, in fact, a formula is provided allowing the House to have the order of the governor in council cancelled that would alter part of a double taxation agreement; that provision is one that can be found in all bills to implement agreements to avoid double taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to add to what I said on second reading of this bill. Mr. Speaker, as a consequence of some of the remarks made by the minister I would just like to point out that the great "built-in protection" in the bill to which he made reference, being the need to submit an order passed by the governor in council to this House for its consideration, has, as an integral part of that protection a form of time limitation, and the minister might well have directed his attention to that rather offensive provision of the bill.
I am speaking, of course, of Clause 9(4) which provides that even though a motion may indeed be referred to the House, it is referred to the House for five hours of debate. We know that this government has an inclination with respect to most legislation which it now brings forward on a regular basis to impose either closure or some form of time limitation. This time limitation is now finding its way into statutes which are passed by the House regularly with respect to tax conventions between Canada and other nations. I recognize that it is important in international tax agreements to have some kind of control over what a rebellious democratically elected Parliament may do from time to time, but that is one of the failings of democracy.
With respect to treaties signed by Canada and submitted to the United States Senate for its consideration-as was the case
with the east coast fishing treaties-the U.S. Senate, being democratically elected, decided it would not grant its approval. However, no time limitation was imposed in the United States with respect to the granting of that approval or the casting of a vote for or against the position of the United States government, even though at the time of entering into that treaty, the government of the United States indicated its support for the proposition which both Canada and the United States adopted.
I therefore find that Subclause (4) of Clause 9 is repugnant to the freedom of debate that should take place in this House with respect to every piece of legislation which is brought forward. This creeping time limitation may eventually give way to a circumstance in which we may well be confronted with 15-minute time limitations to consider any legislation the government may wish to bring forward. What is the purpose of our being here if it is not to reflect wisely-we hope wisely- upon the legislation the government brings before the House? We may well ask ourselves why we do not stay home. Why bother coming to this House, if it is not to debate freely the merit or lack of merit in any government legislation? I find it offensive to be confronted with what appears to be a routine piece of legislation with a built-in time limitation in the form of closure in respect of what should be a non-partisan matter.
May I just comment upon the general scope and effect of my experience of government reaction to the avoidance of double taxation in Canada and other foreign jurisdictions. A moment ago the minister spoke of the negotiations which the Department of Finance and, presumably, Revenue Canada had entered into with the Federal Republic of Germany regarding the very issue of the avoidance of double taxation. We know that such a treaty currently exists. It is not working very well. I can give the minister a piece of information which he might like to carry back to those negotiations with the West Germans.
There has developed a system of avoiding the application of the convention between our two countries, and it is the simple expedient of never issuing an assessment in the foreign jurisdiction. All foreign nations' tax authorities need do is to extract a penalty by way of a deposit against potential future tax liabilities and never issue an assessment.
I have just concluded a meeting with Revenue Canada, the branch which deals with the enforcement, as it were, of our tax convention with West Germany, and some of those officials threw up their hands and said, if the West German authorities would only issue an assessment, they could act. So far, all they have done is to extract $200,000, and they have done nothing with it for nine years.
If tax conventions are to have any real substance and, indeed, prevent double taxation of Canadian residents or Canadian business enterprises-and they should surely be as much our concern as German residents and German business enterprises are the concern of Germany-we must see to it that the effects we wish to produce are in fact produced and that we do not fall into the trap of permitting one of the authorities to evade the real purpose and intent of the conven-
April 14, 1981

tion by never issuing a tax assessment against a Canadian taxpayer.
It is my hope that particular attention will be given in these negotiations of which the minister spoke, to the obvious way of avoiding the intent and purpose of our conventions with foreign nations.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise this evening before our Easter break to speak on behalf of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) on a bill, the sentiments behind which have long been with us; that is, to shorten the election period. I might remind members of the House that this bill is identical, I believe, to a bill presented by the former government, led by the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). I am glad to see the House leader of the official opposition party in the House, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), as I believe it was he who introduced that bill in the previous Parliament.
The bill we are discussing is very short, but it proposes a very important change in our election practices. If passed, the bill will shorten the election period from 60 to 47 days. I am sure many of us in this House who have been through a number of election campaigns, will welcome this shortening of the election period. I have no doubt there will be easy passage of this bill after due consideration, because everyone, I am sure, is interested in the basic principle behind it which is, of course, to shorten the period by some 13 days.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that the shortening of the period will be accomplished by the dispensation of the practice of sending copies of the preliminary voters list to urban households. Instead, a printed notice of enumeration will be mailed to each electorate.
Canada Elections Act
It is important to note that a change of this nature has been discussed for many years. During the last two elections campaigns there were more discussions than ever about the length of the election period.
It is not only parliamentarians who have been concerned about this. I should like to draw your attention to the fact that the Chamber of Commerce, for example, has said that the two-month campaign means-and I am paraphrasing now- that public business is interrupted for quite an extended period. The chamber requested at its 1980 annual meeting that serious consideration be given, when the Canada Elections Act was next before the House for amendment, to shortening the election period.
Many others have contended that our drawn-out election campaigns have not allowed people to focus on the main issues and policies. Instead, public interest is lost and many people are not sufficiently well informed by the time the election date arrives. You may also remember that back in 1973 this House passed amendments to the Canada Elections Act dealing with election expenses. One of the provisions of that amendment was to limit paid advertising by parties to 29 days, I believe, before election day.
The effect of this in the 1979 and 1980 election campaign- because that particular provision was not in effect in 1974- was one of limiting the general focus of the public on the election itself. I am sorry, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton did not understand me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: What did you say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
It was my contention that by restricting the paid election advertising to the last 29 days before an election-I think it was the last 29 days-the public's focus has, I believe, narrowed, so that in effect we do have what amounts to a four or five-week campaign.
What we are saying in this bill is: let us give it some statutory limitation; let us conform to what is in fact becoming a reality, a reality which has occurred because we amended this act previously to take into account the election expenses provisions, which I believe worked quite well in the 1979 and 1980 election and in the byelections since 1976.
During recent elections another form of complaint has also been heard. This complaint concerns the practice of sending copies of the printed preliminary voting list to urban electors. This concerns women particularly. I know my friends on the other side, who have shown a great interest in women's concerns during the constitutional debate, especially my friends in the New Democratic Party, will take this into account in considering the reduction in the length of the election campaign. Many women living alone feel that the voters lists, which are also posted in public places, receive far too wide a circulation. The name, address and sex of each person who has been enumerated are displayed on these posted lists. This information is also available to every person within a polling division, since the printed preliminary list is mailed to each household where the people have been enumerated. Thus, it is possible to find out who lives in all the houses nearby or in all

April 14, 1981
Canada Elections Act
the apartments in a building. It is a simple matter to determine from the list, for example, where there are women living alone. Recently many women's groups have passed resolutions opposing the practice of sending out the preliminary lists. The Canadian Federation of University Women, with a membership of 12,109 people across the country, passed a resolution to this effect at its annual meeting in August, 1980. Various police groups have also stated that they feel the wide circulation given to the lists is a security risk to many people. The bill, if passed, would help to alleviate these sorts of complaints, in addition to shortening the election period. To many people, a change in the practice of mailing preliminary voters' lists is as important, if not more so, than a reduction in the length of the election period.
I speak from personal knowledge. Not only was I on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections from 1976 to 1978 when we were discussing amendments to the Canada Elections Act-and I heard the concerns of the chief electoral officer on this point-but as one who represents an urban constituency in metropolitan Toronto, 50 per cent of which is composed of apartments, I realize this particular problem must be dealt with. I wish the situation would be otherwise, but we must change the Canada Elections Act so that we do not put fear into the hearts of many of our female citizens who do not like the publicity which is now being afforded by these lists. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the provisions of the bill, I should like to review the facts that have led us to introduce these amendments. I have already mentioned some of the criticisms which this legislation would silence. I must also point out that the possibility of shortening the period required to hold a general election has already been considered by the Privy Council's privileges committee. The Chief Electoral Officer submitted a report on ways likely to shorten the election period in which he considered various ways to reduce the time required for drawing up lists of electors.
I noticed that almost all our government colleagues are here tonight and that we have two women members here, but all members opposite are well aware that one of the reasons why our elections are so long is that new lists of electors are drawn up at every election. Many countries do not do this. They use what are called permanent lists or continuing election records.
In his 1975 report, the Chief Electoral Officer did an excellent study on the use of such lists and records. The permanent lists are drawn up or updated once a year only. They have the advantage of being ready as soon as an election is called, but they can also be several months old and be outdated and thus deprive of the right to vote many otherwise eligible voters whose name does not appear on the lists. But on the other hand, the records can be changed at any time or very soon after publication of the writ of election. Both methods are costly because they require permanent or semi-permanent administrative systems to compile and update the lists. In his
1975 report, the Chief Electoral Officer estimated at about $30 million a year the cost of having a system of electoral files which could be regularly updated until an election was held. Of course, the cost would now be much higher.

After reviewing the pros and cons of some form of permanent voters' list, the chief electoral officer suggested that a substantial shortening of the election period could be achieved by eliminating the practice of printing and distributing copies of the preliminary voters' lists to urban electors.
Typesetting and printing these lists by traditional methods is a time-consuming and costly process. It was suggested that voters could be informed of the fact that they are on the list by a notice of enumeration sent to each household. Candidates would still be provided with photocopies of the preliminary lists. The Chief Electoral Officer pointed out in his report that this rather simple change in our election practices could shorten the election period to 47 days in all.
I think 47 days is quite a considerable period of time, especially when we consider the modern age in which we live with mass communications and jet travel. I realize this will impose certain hardships on rural ridings, and I see a couple of members tonight who have particularly large northern ridings. But it is our contention that 47 days would be sufficient in which to conduct the election period.
The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections discussed the report of the Chief Electoral Officer at several meetings in 1976. After extensive questioning and debate, it became clear that the members of the committee did not think the introduction of permanent lists or a continuous electoral roll would be desirable at that time. However, there was considerable support in the committee for the idea of shortening the election period through the elimination of the printing of preliminary lists, as provided in this bill.
On March 23, 1976, a motion to that effect was agreed to in committee. At a later meeting on April 1, 1976, a second motion was passed. In that second motion, the committee recommended that even if the government decided not to reduce the election period, consideration should be given to eliminating the printing of preliminary lists for the reasons we have stated.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, it is important to remember that the bill under consideration takes into account the recommendations which were discussed at length both in a committee of the House and among the general public. It is also appropriate to mention that Bill C-58 is nearly identical to Bill C-21 which was introduced and tabled on November 5, 1979, on behalf of the previous government by my colleague for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the House leader of the official opposition. Only a few very slight technical changes have been made to this bill.
I hope that my colleagues opposite will support the principle of this bill and examine it seriously in the committee. Bill C-58 proposes two major changes in our election practices. First, it
April 14, 1981

will reduce the election period to a minimum of 47 days, which will substantially shorten the length of election campaigns which have lasted something less than 60 days these last few years. A provision of the bill would guarantee a minimum of 11 complete days between the announcement of an election and the beginning of enumeration. In recent elections, according to many people, time has often been very short to recruit and train enumerators. The Chief Electoral Officer has noted for instance that, in 1979, something less than six days passed between the announcement of the election and the beginning of the enumeration. A lapse of eleven days before enumeration would allow the organizations of candidates to recruit enumerators and the returning officers to make these enumerators more familiar with the important work entrusted to them.
The second major change proposed under Bill C-58 will be to stop sending the preliminary lists to the electors. As I have just said it takes a lot of time to print those lists by traditional methods and that is one of the reasons why the electoral periods have always been so long. Instead of the lists the bill proposes that a card be sent to each enumerated voter.
Besides confirming to the elector that his or her name appears on the list this card would provide information on the revision of the lists, the location of the voting poll and the possibility of voting before election day. I should point out that this card would be sent to all electors whether they be in urban or rural ridings. Under current legislation the preliminary voters lists mailed to urban households give among other things the location of the poll, the revision procedures and other detailed information which is not made available to rural riding residents. The bill will help to do away with that serious and long-lasting anomaly.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to make a small number of changes in our election practices. These are not new ideas; they have been studied and discussed since 1976. As I have mentioned, following the past two federal elections, many groups and individual citizens have spoken out in favour of a Canada elections act along the lines of what is contained in this bill.
The government presents this bill in the hope that it will receive support from all parties. The members on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections will, no doubt, study this bill in great detail. I know that they will be assisted in their work by the chief electoral officer, whose 1975 report has helped us greatly in trying to see if there are ways in which our election campaigns could be shortened. The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections may want to suggest changes in Bill C-58, but I sincerely hope that we will be able to bring into effect the changes which are being proposed. As elected members, we must constantly strive to maintain the public's confidence in our electoral process.
Canada Elections Act
I am sure, given the fact that the previous Liberal government, the previous Conservative government and now the present government have all agreed with the principle contained in this bill, that all members will give it speedy passage through the House of Commons so that when we do engage in the next election campaign we will be conducting it in a much more realistic time period of 47 days. I think that will probably bring us more into line with most other countries in the free world which have elections, even those large countries such as the United States, Australia, or other countries like them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
My friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), says that the United States takes a year. Perhaps the U.S. is not the best example. It seemed to me that the campaign in the United States really took place only in the last six weeks before election day.
In any event, in many provincial jurisdictions the period is much shorter. We have just gone through an election campaign in Quebec which took about four weeks, I believe, and a 37-day campaign in Ontario. I think we will all be doing ourselves and the people of Canada a great favour by giving this bill speedy passage through the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
