speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate. At the outset I would like to express concern and disappointment in that the parliamentary secretary did not see fit to answer what I thought was a reasonably straightforward question which might have expedited this matter.

April 14, 1981
Canada Elections Act
He raised a point in the House which at the outset I would like to address, that is, that this bill-and I think I quote him-"would go a long way to increase the confidence in the electoral process". With respect, I dissent. Certainly the purpose of the bill is not to increase the confidence in the electoral process. The bill has absolutely nothing to do with increasing the confidence in the electoral process. I think my good friend the parliamentary secretary overspeaks himself. I find there is a great deal of confidence in the electoral process.
One of the reasons for this bill is precisely one of the things that this bill would cease if it were passed. It is something upon which I have reflected. My friend was absolutely right when he said that I had the privilege of introducing a bill much the same as this one. There have been some changes made to it. I must say to him that at the time I had concerns with respect to the bill and I am now glad that the House will have an opportunity to reflect upon those concerns. One of these concerns is the fact that we have a system in place, in the electoral sense, in which the people do have confidence. That is one thing in which they do have confidence, although they are sometimes a bit shattered by the results of an election. I have spoken to many people who have confidence in the electoral system who find themselves, at the end of an election, saddled with a government which has broken every promise but one. That happens to be the promise about the price of oil. You will recall that one, Mr. Speaker. I see you smiling-you do recall that. Some of us in the country would urge the government to break that one last promise and get it over with so we can settle the impasse which exists in the country with respect to energy pricing. But that is said as an aside.
The process itself is open. It is governed by excellent officials. It ensures not only who people are but it ensures that neighbours, friends, political workers, candidates, official agents and everyone involved in the process who should be on the list is on the list. This is a result of the circulation of the list, the very thing that this bill, if it is passed in its present form, would eliminate. The list is compiled and circulated for a good reason; that is, to ensure the open and notorious aspect of our public elections. I recognize the balance and the concerns that my friend has spoken about; but this does become a balancing of the concerns. I care a lot about the process. It may be that we can accomplish the shortening of elections without eliminating the open and notorious aspect of them. That is why I am disturbed, with the reflection of time, that the bill is so narrow and that we have not yet addressed what was in the Speech from the Throne about electoral reform.
Everyone will recall that Speech from the Throne. I am sure we all recall the promises in it about great things which would be done for the country economically and socially. There would be electoral reform. Remember those words? They talked about proportional representation. We were supposed to deal with that. We were supposed to reform the institutions of Parliament to make them more responsive. We were going to look at the whole electoral process to ensure that all parts of the country were represented. Quite frankly, I am disappointed that what is brought forth here is a bill on a very narrow point
taken out of another government's legislative program and dealing with only one aspect of it; that is, the shortening of election campaigns.
In the course of his speech my friend relied to a great extent, on the period of time for elections in provinces. We all know they are much shorter. I have a list of them here in front of me, but I will not deal with them in detail. It seems to me that the most extensive period of time is in British Columbia, which is about 38 days. I am not at all surprised that provinces have shorter periods of time for elections. I am not the least bit surprised about that. There are ten of them in the country, and they vary in size, complexity, geography, weather, and all the kinds of conditions which affect you and I, Mr. Speaker, as candidates in getting around from place to place to meet real people whom we ask to send us to Parliament. They all have that variation. However, the great difference between a provincial election and a federal election is that, notwithstanding the aeroplane, the automobile, and all the modern means of communication, the problem is multiplied ten times in a national election. So I think for that reason we ought to reflect very carefully on that bill.
As a person who advanced a bill on behalf of the government, I say that we ought to reflect very carefully with respect to that bill before we rush headlong to approve it. It must be explored quite deeply because this House of Commons is an interesting place. My friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette), told us that he represents the riding of York East in which apartment buildings predominate. He said that about 50 per cent of his riding is made up of apartment buildings. Most of the people in his riding, or at least half of his riding, have chosen to go upwards rather than outwards. So, relatively speaking, it makes it quite an easy and uncomplicated task for a member of Parliament or for a candidate in an urban area to deal with that constituency within a short period of time.
However, as people within a riding begin to spread out, and if one moves into suburban ridings, the circumstances may be different. If one goes into rural ridings, there may be even a greater problem. If one goes into the north, where there are great distances to cover and where aeroplanes are required to travel within the riding and covering those distances takes time, then a new set of problems arises which we must accommodate.
We accommodate diversities of language, we accommodate diversities of racial groups, and we accommodate regional diversities within Canada. There are electoral diversities which we must consider as well.
Quite frankly these are matters which cross my mind as I consider that bill. We never did reach that bill in the course of the last Parliament. I am just as happy we did not because of the differences which there are in the country. I am not suggesting that this bill will not ultimately pass, but I do not think we should rush headlong into it. I believe that hon. members who represent different kinds of constituencies have
April 14, 1981

different sorts of electoral problems and should have an opportunity to speak in the debate, because the interesting thing about electoral reform in the House of Commons is that we have usually done it in consultation with each other.
The whole Election Expenses Act was an exercise in mutal assistance as the opposition and the government worked together to produce what I consider to be in principle-it is always subject to change from time to time-a masterpiece in the political process. It is that because all kinds of hon. members participated in that election.
It is no argument to say that this bill follows naturally from the provisions of the Election Expenses Act which requires that advertising begin only after the election campaign has been in process for a period of time. Paid advertising may be placed in newspapers, on television and on the radio only in the last 29 days of an election campaign.
I think the general public will agree with me when I say that 29 days is sufficient time. In terms of financing elections, 29 days is too much, however, in terms of the impact upon the public, I guess that 29 days is enough. People complain to us all the time about their favourite programs being pre-empted and how the election ads in the newspapers and over the radio in their automobiles and in their kitchens as they are working have interfered with their usual listening habits, yet this is all part of getting the message across. But the message is enough. However, if my friend is justifying shortening the election period by using the argument of the shortness of the advertising period, then, I say, with respect, he is comparing apples and oranges. I do not think one necessarily flows from the other. My reason is this. The kinds of advertising I am talking about, the paid advertising, is usually done in Canada on a national party basis. Even the leaders of the party depend upon that. The theme of the campaign, the theme of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the theme of the contender to the job of the Prime Minister is usually done on a national basis. I do not know about you, Mr. Speaker, but within my budget I cannot reasonably afford, in an election campaign under the Election Expenses Act, to have television advertising. I am sure you cannot afford it. I cannot afford to have the giant ads running in the newspapers. I cannot afford radio advertising, except for a very small part of the campaign, nor can any private hon. member in this House do so, because we are all governed by very strict expense provisions, and so be it. It is right that it should be so. This is not a complaint, it is a fact. This is not supposed to be anything else than the House of Commons.
However, what I can do, and what that time allows me as a candidate and everyone in this room to do is to build up, to augment or to develop an organization that works. Where is it, you may ask. Where the people are, on the street. In the context of an election, it allows me as a candidate, or anyone who stands for public office, the time within the election campaign, not to fly over the riding, not to drive through the riding in a motorcade, but to get out in the street and meet the people and to carry on the work that one should do in this business between elections, but to do it within the election
Canada Elections Act
context, when the public mind is focused on the election. That is the importance of time, whether it be in an urban or a suburban constituency.
That is why I think all of us should think very carefully about what we are doing. If we represent rural ridings then there may be another set of problems with which I am only partially familiar. However, they are there. It takes time. There are members now sitting on both sides of this House who represent rural constituencies and who know how much time it takes to go up and down the concession roads, to get out of your car, because one cannot canvass those houses on foot, and go out to meet the farmer, his wife and the members of his family, to get back in your car and get on your way again. No one who has not done it can quite understand the problems. But it all takes time.
I know that our society is becoming urbanized and we are centralizing in cities. But, whatever we do in terms of accommodating potential members of the House of Commons, we must, I think, accommodate the differences which arise with respect to this matter. That is why I do not think we should rush into this adopting this measure and saying it is the greatest thing since sliced bread, because it is not. There will be opinions expressed in the course of this election which will indicate that to the people.
I talked about sending out the lists. I realize there are problems. The parliamentary secretary mentioned some problems that have been brought to my attention, but, I confess, not as forcibly as they may have been brought to his. Even when I was in charge of that bill in the other government, I was not deluged with complaints about the operation of that act. I think we should perhaps work on changing the list and the form of the list. This might be helpful in shortening it.
Why should lists be sent out? It is part of the openness of the election system. It is part of telling people that they are part of a community and who else is in that community. It allows people who live on the street to know who lives up the street and to deal with them on a much more personal basis. It also assists the people who work for parties to assess whether someone who is on the list should be there or whether someone who is not on the list should be on it. It allows friends and neighbours to help others.
Its most important quality is its openness. When only a small number of the lists is produced and they are sent around to only a few people, that has the effect of treating some citizens differently from others. I think in an open election where every vote counts, and only counts once, and every voter is treated equally, they should be treated equally in every part of the process. That is the reason for the list and that is the reason we ought not to move quickly just in order to save some money.
When this bill goes to committee, I hope we will look, for the first time in this Parliament, at the matter of a permanent voters' list. I know this would be expensive but it would be a valuable adjunct to our system. I know it would mean that a

April 14, 1981
Canada Elections Act
number of people would have to be employed to do this, but I think it would be worth while considering, so that we could make sure that the process is as responsive as it possibly can be.
There is another point about the shortened election which some of us, and perhaps most of us in this House, do not think about. That is that it favours incumbents. It is very easy for us to pass on that and say that we should shorten the election but, in effect, it favours the incumbent. I often wonder if that is fair. I look at some of our practices and wonder if they are fair. I think we have to consider that a short time favours the incumbent. If we are to make the process open and if we are to make sure that it is open to everybody on more or less an equal basis, then we must examine every proposal that comes forward to make sure, whether it is with respect to our constituency offices or anything at all, that we do not favour ourselves as incumbents, even if we do so inadvertently. Even if we do that with the best intentions, I think the shortened election campaign favours the incumbent, and we ought to look at it from that point of view.
There are other hon. members who want to speak on this, Mr. Speaker. I said at the outset that I thought it was important that the bill be brought forward if the government thinks it should be. It is regrettable that it is not considered in the context of a host of other things that we should look at in terms of the election, but there is time to do that. There is no great rush that I know of to shorten the election to 47 days unless my hon. friend knows something that I do not. There is time for us to consider not just this little narrow point-and that is all it is, the narrow point-but some of the broader things that our members will be speaking about as the debate goes on.
It is a way of improving the process, not just for those of us who are here but for everyone who might want to be here and to ensure that it is open to everyone else. That is the spirit in which we will approach this debate. It will allow us as Members of Parliament on all sides to speak to the differences that there are in this country. There is a tendency for us to forget the broadness and diversity of the country from time to time.
One thing that being a Member of Parliament of Canada has allowed most of us to do is to get to know our country better and to realize that the issues of Prince Edward Island, say, are different from the issues that concern British Columbia, the prairies or central Canada. We also learn that the conditions are different, the solutions are different and that the law can apply differently, to discriminate among the different regions of the country. If that is the type of thing we have to avoid, I hope there will be expressions from all sides of the House about how this bill will affect the regions from which members come, the constituencies which are different and the problems which are different.
This is a blanket piece of legislation, whether your constituency happens to be in British Columbia, Ontario, downtown Toronto or somewhere north of sixty. That is the proposition we are going to apply to the whole diverse country of Canada. That is the spirit in which we will approach this debate.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) told us at a House leaders' meeting that he proposed to bring forward this bill, I confess that I made an immediate and personal response. I said, what about making it retroactive for the last 16 elections? I have done a little arithmetic and realize that it would have added quite a bit to my life if we could have taken out 13 days from each of the last 16 federal elections in which I have been a candidate. Although that statement makes the point that candidates are concerned about the length of the election, the people who have the greatest interest are the voters of Canada. What we have to come to is a judgment on whether they like elections that last eight or nine weeks or whether they would like them a little shorter. I believe that the general view is that our election campaigns are too long; that they are such that toward the end of the campaign many people lose interest or feel that the same arguments are being thrown back and forth among the contending parties, and if we could cut the time by a couple of weeks it would be better for the process.
I agree with my hon. friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that there is no final arbitrator who can say what length of time would be best. I suppose we cannot really tell until we have tried the shorter as well as the longer. But I express the view, that as I see it the people of Canada would approve of shortening the election campaign.
I remember that in 1979, after we had gone out of here, the House having been dissolved, the British Parliament was also dissolved. They held an election and their Parliament sat again while we were still out on the hustings. I know that the area of Great Britain is minuscule compared with ours, but that country has twice as many people and elects twice as many members as we do. It also has had twice as much experience as we have had with electing members to a democratic Parliament.
My friend across the way said his face turned red when he was talking about shorter elections. Thank God we do not have the United States system which results in elections lasting for about a year at a time. As a matter of fact, I sometimes wonder about the sense of their electing members to the House of Representatives for a term of only two years when they campaign for about a year. When do they get down to business? At any rate, it seems to me that we would improve the process if we had a shorter period. After all, the proposal in this bill for 47 days does not make it extremely short. It is still longer than any of the elections held in any of the provinces. However, I would hope the idea might be given some consideration.
Let me say right away that I agree with the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton that this is a matter which should be arrived at by consensus. This has been the practice about amendments to the Canada Elections Act down through the years. We usually wait a few months after an election, some-
April 14, 1981

times into the second session. But we are now into the second year, even if we are not into the second session. At any rate whatever changes are made, they are studied very carefully in committee, and I hope we will find a way to adopt that practice in so far as this matter is concerned.
I say with respect to my colleagues in the New Democratic Party that the same differences exist among their ridings as those to which the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton referred in his remarks. After all, I have a constituency that I can walk around in a few hours. I believe it measures about eight square miles. On the other hand, my friend, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), has an area which is larger than 15 or 20 countries in some parts of the world. Then there is my friend from Churchill and my friend from Skeena with large distances to cover in their ridings. There are others who have these far-flung ridings. As a matter of fact, you do not have to go to the north to find far-flung ridings. In the heart of Manitoba there is the constituency of Selkirk-Interlake. And so it goes. It is only natural that with these different conditions members will have different views.
I may say also there is some concern about what is to be done with respect to the lists. I believe there have been meetings among the bureaucrats of our various parties, persons who are not members of the House at all but who get called into action when there is an election. They have some joint concerns, and these matters could well be looked at by the committee. But I feel very strongly that these differences of views and the need for consensus and the need to study the details of this bill and even to consider other ways to achieve a shorter election period should not stop us from going ahead with this matter.
I gather from what my friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, said, that there are other members in his party who wish to speak, so that my sitting down now or my sitting down at one minute to ten o'clock would not result in the bill receiving second reading tonight. I see that opinion confirmed by the nod of the head from my friend from Nepean-Carleton.
I hope there might be some interparty consultation about this, maybe among the House leaders or maybe among the persons most concerned, in our parties. I hesitate to make the following suggestion, but I throw it into the pot along with all of the others, namely, that if it is felt that some of the details in the bill are not quite what some members want, then maybe instead of sending the bill to committee we could send the subject matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. My hon. friend from Nepean-Carleton says he does not think there is any hurry. That is what he thought on December 10 or December 11 a year ago. He knows what happened then.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: You thought there was a hurry and you know what happened.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
There probably is not a situation like that one now, but time does have a way of going on. Just because the next election may not be until 1984 or 1985, that does not
Canada Elections Act
mean we have all kinds of time. This is 1981, and time marches on.
I hope in one way or the other that we will convey this idea of a shorter election period to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so it can be considered there. I expressed the view that I think the judgment of the people of Canada will be with us, in other words, that a shorter election would be better for the process. That, of course, does not set aside all of the other things in the process to which my hon. friend referred. That does not set aside the extreme importance of the result of the election, but as between a long-drawn-out election of about nine weeks and an election of about seven weeks, I believe the preference of the people of Canada would be for the shorter election.
Therefore, I speak in support of the principle of the bill, although, as I say, our colleagues on the committee will want to go into the various details of it. I hope that before we are finished with this bill we will have arrangements for a shorter and more compact election period the next time members are sent out onto the hustings.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might indicate at the outset that I have to concur with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he indicated his belief in his reading of the electorate generally with respect to the time during which elections are held in Canada. I would like to think as well that my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), when he was expressing his concerns with respect to the lists, had not overlooked the other principles in the bill, in particular the reduction of the time period, and that there would be some concurrence in his mind as well. I notice he nods his head affirmatively that the principle of reducing the time period from what has been the historic practice in Canada to something shorter, perhaps to 47 days, which has no magic to it, but is an attempt to reflect the concerns of the electorate generally, has, up to this point, been viewed as being too long.
With respect to my other hon. friend who asked the parliamentary secretary where the concerns about the elections had come from, I ask him to recall the last campaign. Perhaps he might remember that even his campaign workers, particularly during the last two or three weeks of the campaign, heard comments that people really felt they had heard it all before. Television and radio announcements and comments at various all-party meetings and all-candidates meetings were old hat. People had had the opportunity already to reflect on the issues being put forward by the various party leaders. They were already in a position to express themselves and needed no further time to do so.
My hon. friend from Nepean-Carleton pointed out that there are distinctions and differences with respect to various ridings. It is interesting that three of us speaking this evening come from Ontario, and yet all three of us represent ridings which are rather different in their makeup. The first speaker, my colleague, the parliamentary secretary, represents a riding which is essentially densely populated by high rise towers but spreads out hardly at all. My colleague from Nepean-Carleton

April 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
represents a riding which perhaps spreads out somewhat farther but does not have as many high rises as the riding of York East. My riding, out of a total number of 180 and some odd polls, has only 20 urban polls in the whole riding. With respect to the rural areas and the necessity for the openness and notoriety of the lists, my hon. friend from Nepean-Carleton points out a difference. I want to put something on the record on which I ask my hon. friends to reflect. My urban friends consider that the stability of the population in rural ridings is a benefit.

subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-NORTH SYDNEY, N.S. TO ARGENT1A, NFLD. FERRY SERVICE

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-NORTH SYDNEY, N.S. TO ARGENT1A, NFLD. FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with reference to an answer to a question given to me yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). The minister has developed a policy which is even more punishing to Atlantic Canada and Canadians who are dependent upon transportation than his predecessor, Otto Lang. Mr. Lang excelled in the user-pay principle, but the present minister has come up with a new principle. Transportation needs are to be decided on something called the multimodal principle.
There is a transportation envelope for each province and there have to be trade-offs within that envelope for each province. In other words, he has said that the transportation
envelope for Newfoundland will be $210 million a year. To give one example, he said to the Newfoundland government that if they want money spent on the Trans-Canada highway and other roads in Newfoundland this year, or on any transportation service, they will get it by permitting us to discontinue some service now being provided to Newfoundland.
The service the minister has chosen is the ferry service in summer from North Sydney to Argentia in Placentia Bay. He said eliminating this ferry service will save $8 million to $9 million a year. The Newfoundland government and people can then decide what other transportation mode they want it spent on. That is the new policy. The new minister is the Jack the Ripper of Canadian transportation policy, Jean-Luc the Ripper.
With the discontinuance of the Argentia-North Sydney ferry service, 300 jobs would be lost in Newfoundland. The minister is from central Canada where they have all the modes of transportation they need. All modes are efficient modes and they have been built up over 100 years. However, in the Atlantic provinces we do not have satisfactory multimodes or any mode of transportation.
In the envelope for Newfoundland, the minister is including the Cabot Strait ferry service which is required by the terms of union. Presumably he is including all road spending, the Trans-Canada Highway, the subsidies for the coastal steamship service, subsidies on the shipping service by Clark from Montreal to St. John's, the new shipping service from St. John's to Goose Bay where there is a CN marine scandal because they gave the contract under false tendering practices to a Liberal friend, Mr. Woodward of Coastal Shipping Limited, a contract which is now being investigated.
They are including airport spending in Newfoundland, the Newfoundland railway expenditure, VIA Rail bus service across Newfoundland, ferry service to Bell Island, St. Barbe to Blanc-Sablon, Change Islands and so on. They are including navigational service, the marine traffic control centres, ferry services. All these services are included in this envelope.
The people of Newfoundland are told that if they want an improvement in the Trans-Canada highway, their airport services, coastal steamship services and ferry services, they have to permit the government to discontinue spending somewhere else.
The Sullivan royal commission on transportation in Newfoundland did not recommend discontinuance of the Argentia to North Sydney service. They suggested that it continue with improvements. I want to point out to the minister that the MacPherson royal commission of 1961 said that the situation in Newfoundland, "Is a special case distinct from the rest of Canada". But the minister wants to take us in Newfoundland, ignore this special situation and say that we are going to be treated in the same multimodal, trade-off, envelope way as Ontario, Quebec or the rest of Canada. Well, it will not work, and the people of Newfoundland will not accept it, the municipal councils will not accept it, the people of the Argentia-Pla-centia area will not accept it, I will not accept it, the Newfoundland government will not accept it, and if the five Liberal
April 14, 1981

MPs who represent other Newfoundland districts here in this House accept it and promote it, they will go down to defeat in the next election, believe me, Mr. Speaker. We are not going to accept it.
We traded off a number of years ago the railway passenger service in Newfoundland. It was a trade-off to get the federal government to assist in spending on the Trans-Canada highway. What we got in return was a bus service from St. John's to Port aux Basques that is inferior in many ways. It never satisfactorily replaced the rail service.
I urge the minister to stop this approach to Newfoundland. We need all of the modes improved in Newfoundland, not one mode set off against the other, not less spending on one if you want more spending on the other. The minister has sunk the synchrolift at the urging of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey). He terminated the Trans-Canada highway agreement. We do not know if he is going to start it again. He is teasing Torbay airport, doing relatively little for it. He has harpooned the harbour improvements in St. John's. This minister is a veritable Jean-Luc the Ripper. That may be all right here in central Canada and Toronto, but even in Toronto he proposes spending $300 million over the next ten years in improvements to the Toronto airport, doubtless needed. I agree that that is a needed expenditure. I will not even mention Mirabel. But he is down gutting our little province saying there is a $210 million transportation envelope, as though this was a gigantic amount when it is very, very little when you divide it among air services, coastal services, ferry services, marine services, water carrier services and the many needs of a province of 48,000 square miles on the island and 110,000 square miles on the mainland of Labrador, with all that implies in scattered communities and transportation needs.
I am asking the minister now-he has affirmed that the Argentia to North Sydney ferry service will continue this summer-to drop this kind of policy in Newfoundland, to make available to Newfoundland perhaps another $80 million to $90 million to enter into a Trans-Canada highway strengthening agreement. The highway is in a desperate condition. We need another three-year agreement, 75 per cent-25 per cent from the federal government. Stop trying to impose this new idea of trade-offs with the people of Newfoundland.
He is going to make Cape Breton suffer, by the way. The representative from North Sydney is in the chamber tonight, and if he wants to help his area in North Sydney, he will do his best to see that this ferry service is not discontinued.
So I hope the parliamentary secretary when he answers tonight will tell me that this ludicrous proposal is going to be dropped, because if it is not dropped, the howl of outrage and protest from Newfoundland is going to give that gentleman quite a lot to do. He will have to do a lot of travelling in Newfoundland this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-NORTH SYDNEY, N.S. TO ARGENT1A, NFLD. FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member gets
Adjournment Debate
more alarmed about these issues, let me assure him that no decision has been made either with respect to terminating the Argentia ferry or with respect to a new highway strengthening program.
I realize that in the first case he does not want a decision and in the second case he does. It should be some comfort to him at least that the Argentia ferry is assured of sailing as usual this summer.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has been at pains to explain to him, what is happening is a series of discussions with the province of Newfoundland and the other Atlantic provinces aimed at finding the best uses for the limited amount of federal money available.
The hon. member seems to get terribly excited when the minister mentions the idea of an envelope and trade-offs. This reaction is quite remarkable, since the hon. member himself spawned the idea.
When the hon. member asked the question yesterday, he said that "the people of Newfoundland know what the minister is trying to do to them, eliminate a service here and then spend the money somewhere else". I would like to quote from a document I happen to have on file. It describes a new system for controlling government spending. It says that the system:
-is intended to focus attention on the hard choices to be made and the trade-offs among alternative policy actions.
It talks about the need to "establish known limits". It says that "the creation of resource envelopes is central to the new system".
Perhaps the hon. member recognizes the document. He should, because he tabled it in the House in December of 1979 when he was minister of finance. So all this is really a great compliment to him. The Minister of Transport recognizes the value of the system proposed by the hon. member and is doing his best to implement it rapidly.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORTATION-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-HOLDING OF INQUIRY
MARINE TRANSPORTATION-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-HOLDING OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 12, 1981, I had the opportunity to address some questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in respect of the withdrawal of Dart Containerline service from the port of Halifax.
My main concern at that time was twofold. First I wanted to ask the minister whether he was in fact ordering an inquiry under the Canadian Transport Commission into the withdrawal of Dart Containerline service from the port of Halifax and, second, I wanted him to consider the role of the Crown agencies, the Canadian National Railways and the National Harbours Board, in relation to the operation of container services in the port of Halifax and the port of Montreal. I was concerned, as were many people in the port of Halifax, that the CNR, in conjunction with the activities of the National

April 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Harbours Board, had permitted this removal of Dart from the port of Halifax to the benefit of the port of Montreal.
The minister, much to my surprise, indicated that there was to be no such inquiry under the National Transportation Act of the kind we in Nova Scotia had envisaged. In fact, the Premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. John Buchanan who had been in Ottawa a few days before, had spoken to the Minister of Transport, and had come away with the impression that there was to be a general inquiry into the activities of container traffic in the North Atlantic using both the ports of Montreal and Halifax, as well as other ports, including the port of Saint John. In fact, in relation to the matter of the inquiry, the minister was simply referring to Section 27 of the National Transportation Act which requires that when a railway company acquires an interest in a shipping company, the acquisition must be brought before the Canadian Transport Commission for examination and approval.
What is happening in this instance is that CP ships are acquiring, or are in the process of acquiring, an interest in Dart Containerline services, and it is the acquisition of that interest by CP ships that has attracted Dart to the port of Montreal.
This matter has to be reviewed by the Canadian Transport Commission, and that will be the subject matter of the inquiry. We do not know how broad that inquiry will be. It is very important for those of us who are interested in the port of Halifax to have the opportunity to present to the Canadian Transport Commission all the factors that have to be taken into account.
What is happening is this. The port of Montreal for the last number of years has been experiencing some difficulty in attracting the large container vessels which are now being employed in the North Atlantic and worldwide marine container traffic. Apparently this has resulted in severe difficulties for shipping companies like CP and Manchester Lines which have seen their north Atlantic traffic drop off. This is the motivation for those companies to become more active and aggressive in acquiring part of the north Atlantic container traffic and has led to moves such as the acquisition of an interest in Dart.
We are concerned because we who are interested in the port of Halifax see some sinister elements in this. In the first place, Canadian National Railways operates the only railway link between Halifax, Montreal and other westward points. The Canadian National Railways last fall, in accordance with an agreement drawn up some years before, acquired an interest in the CAST shipping group. This is an equity interest. It makes CN an owner in the CAST shipping group. It has the right, under its agreements, to acquire a very substantial ownership in the CAST shipping group.
This has caused some concern among other shipping companies, such as Hapag Lloyd, as well as Dart and other international marine transport companies. They are concerned that
this unhealthy liaison between CNR and CAST may result in unfair competition to other north Atlantic carriers.
Many of us think that this is what motivated the move by DART to form a liaison with CP Ships. We think all of this ought to be reviewed very carefully and very closely by the Canadian Transport Commission. We are disappointed that the minister has not seen fit to exercise his authority and power under the act through the Canadian Transport Commission by holding a general inquiry to determine whether these activities-that is the liaison between CP Ships and Dart Containerline service, on the one hand, and the liaison between the CAST shipping group and the CNR on the other-are not detrimental to the public interest in terms of competition in international container traffic.
We are mainly concerned because of the great opportunity this gives the port of Montreal. This brings up the role of the National Harbours Board. We wonder what the National Harbours Board is up to. It appears that some time ago, with the help and co-operation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), they were busily engaged in expanding very dramatically container terminals in the port of Montreal, both on behalf of the CAST group at the Task Terminal and on behalf of CP Ships in relation to the Racine Terminal. We wonder whether this was a plan and program to expand container traffic in the port of Montreal at the expense of the port of Halifax. We want and need an inquiry.
There are many people in Halifax associated with container traffic operations of Halterm and with the container traffic operations of CNR on the land side who say that no inquiry is necessary. I say to those people that what is happening is not in the best interest of the port of Halifax. It is an attempt to cover up what is going on. Those of us who are interested in the welfare of the port of Halifax want all facts to be brought before our national organization, the Canadian Transport Commission, so that everybody knows what is going on, everybody can see what is happening and can make their objections. It may well be that this whole move from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal and the consolidation of container traffic within the port of Montreal are not in the Canadian interest. We want the minister to answer for that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORTATION-WITHDRAWAL OF DART CONTAINERLINE SERVICE FROM HALIFAX-HOLDING OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last month there have been several statements in the House on the subject of the hon. member's question. On March 10, I answered a late show question put by his colleague across the Halifax harbour. On March 17, during an opposition day debate, the minister went into considerable detail on the port of Halifax. So, tonight I will simply review the main points of this issue.
The minister indicated that he will not order an inquiry into the Dart move, but that several opportunities exist for those who wish to intervene formally in front of the Canadian Transport Commission.
At his meeting last month with Premier Buchanan, the minister agreed to undertake some further study into the questions of rail freight rates and icebreaking services on the
April 14, 1981

St. Lawrence. But he pointed out that increases in Halifax-Montreal freight rates over the last ten years were considerably smaller than increases in comparable rates and clearly smaller than increases in the consumer price index. The cost of icebreaking services, to the extent that they could be assessed, would represent a negligible impact on the flow of container traffic.
The other aspect which has been raised is the question of port charges. It is a fact that harbour dues, berthage and wharfage charges are identical for all east coast ports. So there is no discrimination against Halifax. In fact, Halterm enjoys a 50 per cent rebate from the National Harbours Board on wharfage charges, a rebate which amounted to a subsidy of $1.8 million in 1980. It is true that the National Harbours Board intends to raise the land rental rate for Halterm, but Halterm has enoyed a fixed rate of 15 cents per square foot for ten years. The new rate has been determined in exactly the same manner for lessees at all NHB sites.
In summary, most people recognize that in spite of the move of Dart, the port of Halifax retains great promise. The president of Halterm, who stands to lose the most, has rejected the idea of government intervention, and the executive director of the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Commission has painted an optimistic picture of the port's future.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-APPLICATION OF PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH REGIONAL INEQUALITIES
REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-APPLICATION OF PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH REGIONAL INEQUALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my participation in this evening's proceedings arise out of a question which I asked of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on February 12, 1981. It concerned the designation of the manufacturers' tax credit program which was announced in the budget of last October. The criteria which have been used to determine the base for that program is what I was specifically questioning. I felt it was particularly pertinent that there were several areas in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and other regions of Atlantic Canada which qualified under the criteria that were made available to the House under the proposed program.
The fact of the matter is that apparently all of this is being managed under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which has been in place for a number of years. In that regard I would like to draw a brief history of the program of DREE to the attention of the House, how it originated and what it was intended to accomplish, and then provide to the government a proposal which I think would be much more effective than that which, in my opinion, DREE has not been able to accomplish over the years that it has been in place.
Regional disparities, back in the 1950s, were recognized as being something the government should come to grips with. One of the first programs the government of the day implemented was a program of equalization payments. The purpose of these was to reduce to some extent the difficulties that regional disparities were creating in the country. There were a
Adjournment Debate
good many programs which developed after that, including the Agricultural and Rural Development Act, commonly known as ARDA, the Fund for Rural Economic Development, which was known as FRED, the Atlantic Development Board was created, the Area Development Incentives Act was brought before the House and, finally DREE was created.
The purpose of DREE at that stage was to co-ordinate the rest of these programs under one central authority. However, the principal purpose of DREE at that time was to concentrate on the development of those regions of the country which the government felt were in a state of regional disparity. Then after DREE was formed, it undertook an umbrella-like initiative, which included the Regional Development Incentives Act. This act was an inducement to manufacturers to locate in particular regions.
I suggest that DREE has been nothing more than a stop-gap department and it has provided nothing more than band-aid programs and band-aid assistance to certain regions of Canada which have not been long lasting or of any meaningful advantage to the area.
I would like to suggest to the government that people in Atlantic Canada-and I see here the parliamentary secretary from the Atlantic region who cares about what happens there and who will respond to what I am saying-would like to see something much more meaningful than the band-aid approach which has been promoted by DREE over the past several years. They would like to see something which will have a lasting effect. In this regard I would like to suggest that Atlantic Canada be set up as a specifically designated area by the federal government in its negotiations for special trade and tariff recognition in its agreement with the United States. We are geographically a part of that vast market of 48 million people-twice the size of Canada's population. There are 48 million people in New England who are our natural trading partners. If we were to develop a program which recognized the contribution that Atlantic Canada could make to the rest of Canada by giving a specific advantage to that area to manufacturers so that they would locate in that region for reasons of trade with the New England states, I believe that a lasting contribution could be made to Canada by Atlantic Canadians. It would withdraw them from the over-protective attitude of the government which seems to say, "Equalization payments will take care of all your needs", it would reduce the terrifically high unemployment there, and it would be something of lasting value for Atlantic Canada in its contribution to the prosperity and future development of Canada as a whole.
I think that is the approach which they should be taking rather than continuing on with what I refer to as band-aid programs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-APPLICATION OF PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH REGIONAL INEQUALITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister has been asked many times by hon. members in this House why their constituencies have not been designated to receive the benefit of the Special Investment Tax Credit

April 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Program. I am beginning to derive considerable satisfaction from the importance they attach to this bold and innovative program. Most recently the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) asked why more areas in New Brunswick had not qualified for this tax credit.
I will explain to him again the criteria that were used for designation. I will do so in order that he and other hon. members of the House will fully understand the justifiable bases on which these designations were made.
We, on this side, are concerned about people. We are concerned particularly about those who suffer the most economically, living as they do in areas where family unemployment rates are significantly above the national average and where per capita incomes are lowest in relation to the national average.
The Special Investment Tax Credit Program is designated to give these people a hand, by making it worth while for successful and profitable firms to locate in these areas and to provide them with the employment and other economic opportunities that they have lacked for so long.
But we are also cognizant of the need for fiscal restraint. Therefore, with reluctance, we decided to limit the benefits of the program to the 5 per cent of the Canadian population most in need.
It will be obvious to the hon. member opposite, and to others, that not all areas of Canada, and particularly not all of the Atlantic region, could be designated in the light of this contraint. Being from the Atlantic region, I would like to see more parts of it designated, but obviously this would not be equitable in relation to needs elsewhere.
The first point I would like to make in response to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal is that I, too, would like to see other parts of New Brunswick designated. Perhaps this will be possible in the future if the optimism which the hon. member holds for this program, and which I share, materializes in the form of proven success.
The second point I would like to make is that the SITCP is an incentive program. It is a challenge to the private sector to create jobs. But mostly it is a challenge to create jobs in areas where the need is greatest.
The member for Fundy-Royal has asked why more areas were not designated in New Brunswick. The answer is simple.
